questions.title: Distinct prime factors of 52,500
questions.statement: How many prime numbers between 1 and 175 are factors of 52,500?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\20240908_103807.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0096.jpeg
questions.explanation: 52,500 = 2² × 3 × 5⁴ × 7. Its distinct prime factors are 2, 3, 5 and 7, all between 1 and 175.

questions.title: Length of a rectangular garden
questions.statement: A rectangular garden is five times as long as it is wide. If 2,160 yards of fencing, including the gate, completely enclose the garden, what is its length in yards?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0055.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0057.jpeg
questions.explanation: Let width be w and length 5w. Then 2(w+5w)=2,160, so w=180 and length=900 yards.

questions.title: Two rolls with the same face label
questions.statement: A cubical die is marked x on three faces, y on two faces and z on the remaining face. If the die is rolled twice, what is the probability that the first and second rolls show the same label?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_162727188_HDR_AE.jpg
questions.explanation: Assuming a fair die and independent rolls, P(same)=(3/6)²+(2/6)²+(1/6)²=14/36=7/18.

questions.title: Identify a two-pointer array operation
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_162156765_HDR_AE.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_162234882_HDR_AE.jpg

Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0107.jpg
questions.explanation: The function swaps symmetric elements and moves the two indices towards the centre. It reverses the inclusive subarray arr[start…end]; it reverses the entire array when the caller passes its first and last indices. O(end−start+1) time and O(1) space.
options: Traverse each alternate elements of the array.
Swap all alternate elements of the array.
Traverse each and every elements of the array.

questions.title: Minimum digits in a repeated digit-sum chain
questions.statement:
For a natural number n, define f(n) as the sum of its digits. A natural number k satisfies f(f(f(f(k))))=1 and

k > f(k) > f(f(k)) > f(f(f(k))) > 1.

What is the least number of digits that k can have?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Arpwood Capital\arpwood capital (1).pdf
questions.explanation: The smallest value greater than 1 whose digit sum is 1 is 10. The smallest larger number with digit sum 10 is 19; the smallest larger number with digit sum 19 is 199. Thus f(k)≥199, requiring at least ceil(199/9)=23 digits. A 23-digit number with digit sum 199 exists, for example 22 nines followed by 1, so the lower bound is attainable.

questions.title: Expected overlapping HH pairs
questions.statement: A coin is tossed eight times and the outcomes are written as a string. What is the expected number of occurrences of HH? Overlaps count: HHH contains two occurrences of HH.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Arpwood Capital\arpwood capital (1).pdf
questions.explanation: Assuming independent fair tosses, there are seven adjacent pairs. Each is HH with probability 1/4. By linearity of expectation, the expected count is 7/4; independence of overlapping pair indicators is not required.

questions.title: A die is rerolled only after 1, 2 or 3
questions.statement: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. If the first result is 1, 2 or 3, the die is rolled a second time. What is the probability that the sum of all values rolled is at least 6?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Arpwood Capital\arpwood capital (1).pdf
questions.explanation: A first roll of 6 succeeds directly: probability 1/6. First rolls 1, 2 and 3 need second rolls at least 5, 4 and 3, giving 2+3+4 favourable two-roll outcomes out of 36. Total = 1/6 + 9/36 = 5/12.

questions.title: Which divisor counts can belong to a perfect cube?
questions.statement: Numbers A, B, C and D have 22, 37, 53 and 66 positive factors respectively. Which of these could be a perfect cube?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Arpwood Capital\arpwood capital (1).pdf
questions.explanation: A perfect cube has prime exponents 3a, so its divisor count is a product of factors 3a+1, hence is 1 modulo 3. Counts 53 and 66 fail this necessary condition. Counts 22 and 37 are achievable by p²¹ and p³⁶, respectively.
questions.notes: A handwritten mark in the source selects a different answer. The solution here is derived independently.

questions.title: Five-digit multiples of 15 with distinct digits
questions.statement: How many five-digit numbers with distinct digits, divisible by 15, can be formed from the digits 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Arpwood Capital\arpwood capital (1).pdf
questions.explanation: Divisibility by 5 forces the last digit to be 5. The sum of all six available digits is 27. The omitted digit must be 3 or 6 so the five chosen digits sum to a multiple of 3. Each of these two choices has 4! arrangements for the first four positions: 2×24=48.

questions.title: Count printed 3s and 5s
questions.statement: If every integer from 1,000 through 10,000 is printed once, how many occurrences of the digits 3 and 5 are printed in total?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Arpwood Capital\arpwood capital (1).pdf

questions.title: Repeated draws of digit pairs with product 18

questions.title: Expected random-walk steps across a cube

questions.title: Maximum test-window efficiency
questions.statement: Each test has an integer arrival time. Activate the testing environment once from time t₁ to t₂, inclusive; all tests arriving in this interval execute. Efficiency is the number of executed tests minus (t₂−t₁). At least two tests must execute. Return the maximum possible efficiency. Tests sharing an arrival time execute simultaneously, and efficiency may be negative.

Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Expedia\expedia2.jpg

It suffices to activate at arrival endpoints. With repeated timestamps, starting earlier or ending later within a duplicate group only improves the count; the global optimum includes the whole group. O(n log n) time for sorting, O(n) space for a copy.

examples.explanation: Activate from 5 to 6: two tests minus one time unit gives efficiency 1.

questions.title: Count perfect pairs using absolute values
questions.statement:
A pair (x, y) is perfect when both conditions hold:

$\min(|x-y|,|x+y|) \le \min(|x|,|y|)$

$\max(|x-y|,|x+y|) \ge \max(|x|,|y|)$.

Given an integer array arr, count pairs of indices i < j for which (arr[i], arr[j]) is perfect.

Sort absolute values; for each right endpoint, advance the left pointer until this inequality holds, then add right−left. Two zeros form a perfect pair; zero with a nonzero value does not. O(n log n) time and O(n) space for a sorted copy.

questions.title: Maximize weighted panel output with one relocation
questions.statement: For panel outputs X₁…Xₙ, total power is Σ i×Xᵢ using one-based indices. Outputs can be positive or negative. At most once, remove one panel and insert it before or after another panel while preserving the order of all remaining panels. Return the maximum total power.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Myntra\IMG_20240828_172913.pdf
questions.explanation: Compute prefix sums P and the original weighted sum. Moving panel i right to j changes it by (j−i)Xᵢ−(P[j]−P[i]); moving it left to j changes it by (j−i)Xᵢ+P[i−1]−P[j−1]. Maximize these gains and include zero gain. Enumerating i,j gives O(N²) time and O(N) space. For large N, prefix/suffix sweeps with a maximum-line data structure answer the corresponding j×Xᵢ−P[j] or j×Xᵢ−P[j−1] queries in O(N log N).
questions.notes: Numeric upper bounds are not visible in the PDF; select the optimized approach if quadratic work is too large.

questions.title: Count straight word occurrences in eight directions
questions.statement: Given an N×N character grid and a word, count its occurrences along horizontal, vertical and diagonal straight lines in either direction. Reverse directions count separately, so a palindromic occurrence is counted in both orientations. The grid may contain uppercase letters, lowercase letters and digits.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\mastercard\IMG-20240812-WA0013.jpg

Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\mastercard\IMG-20240812-WA0019.jpg
questions.explanation: Try every starting cell and each of the eight direction vectors. Check that the ending coordinate is inside the grid, then compare successive characters along that direction. Increment once for each complete match; do not deduplicate opposite directions for palindromes. O(N²×word_length) time and O(1) additional space. Preserve character case unless the complete input specification says otherwise.
questions.input_format: N, followed by N grid rows, followed by the word.
questions.output_format: The occurrence count.
questions.constraints: N ≥ 3; no upper bound is visible.
questions.notes: The source does not explicitly define case folding or the direction-count convention for a one-character word. The visible sample uses exact character matches.

questions.title: Sum binary-tree supernodes defined by child digit sums
questions.statement: A binary tree is represented by its root value and path-labelled nodes: L/R means left/right from the root, and longer paths such as LL or RRL continue those steps. A node is a supernode if it has both children and the sum of decimal digits of its left child equals that of its right child. Return the sum of the values of all supernodes.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\mastercard\IMG-20240812-WA0016.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\mastercard\IMG-20240812-WA0017.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\mastercard\IMG-20240812-WA0020.jpg
questions.explanation: Store each node value under its root-relative path, with the root at the empty path. For every path p with both p+L and p+R present, compare their digit sums and add the parent value when equal. Leaves and one-child nodes cannot qualify. O(total path characters+N×D) time and O(total path characters) space, where D is the largest digit count.
questions.input_format: N, root value, then N−1 lines containing path and node value.
questions.output_format: The sum of supernode values.

questions.title: Evaluate criteria for choosing a nonrelational database
questions.statement:
Which of these criteria is unsuitable as a reason to choose a nonrelational database?

- Very low application latency
- Unstructured data without relationships
- Only serialization/deserialization of JSON, XML or YAML
- Storing a very small amount of data

questions.explanation: Store only nonzero entries rather than a dense n×n matrix. An adjacency-list representation records each row’s nonzero columns and values; symmetry can let you keep one triangle and reconstruct the other. Compressed sparse-row or coordinate formats are also common. A hash table keyed by (row,column) is another sparse representation, so the most efficient choice depends on lookup/update and traversal needs. Among the listed options, adjacency list is the conventional graph-style answer.
questions.notes: The MCQ does not define the operations or storage layout needed to distinguish adjacency lists from hash-based sparse storage.

questions.title: Assess comparisons between a 2–3 tree and a BST

The source asks which statement is false:

1. A 2–3 tree requires less storage than a BST.
2. Lookup in a 2–3 tree is more efficient than in a BST.
3. A 2–3 tree is shallower than a BST.
4. A 2–3 tree is balanced.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240730-WA0078.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0090.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\ORACLE-MCQ-Final.pdf
questions.explanation: A 2–3 tree keeps every leaf at the same depth and has logarithmic height. An unbalanced BST can become a linear chain, so a 2–3 tree has better worst-case lookup against that baseline. A balanced BST also gives O(log n) lookup. Total memory depends on node layout, pointer counts and occupancy, so the claim of always requiring less storage is unjustified. The likely intended false statement is 1, but statements 2 and 3 also need a stated BST baseline.
questions.notes: The source does not specify whether its BST is balanced or how storage is measured.

questions.title: Interpret ambiguous sports-survey totals
questions.statement: A source MCQ says that 100 selected employees include 50 who like football, 40 who like hockey, and “the rest like both.” It asks how many like at least one game. Options: 40, 90, 80, 20.

Treating “the rest” as 100−50−40=10 gives 80, but then 20 employees like neither, contradicting a literal claim that every remaining employee likes both. If 50 and 40 mean exclusive categories and the remaining 10 like both, everyone likes at least one, giving 100, which is absent. Thus 80 is a plausible intended answer under an extra assumption, not a logically unambiguous consequence.

questions.explanation: The final postorder value is the root. Its unique position in inorder separates the left and right subtrees, which can then be reconstructed recursively. Distinct values are necessary for this simple uniqueness guarantee. Preorder plus postorder does not distinguish a lone left child from a lone right child; the other supplied pairs have similar ambiguities for general binary trees.
questions.notes: The source does not state the distinct-values assumption; it is made explicit here.

questions.title: Purpose of rotations in an AVL tree
questions.statement: What is the primary purpose of rotations in an AVL tree?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0037.jpg
questions.explanation: Rotations restore the AVL invariant that the two child-subtree heights differ by at most one while preserving BST inorder ordering. This keeps height O(log n), supporting logarithmic search, insertion and deletion. It does not require a complete tree or equal depth for every leaf.
options: Put all leaves at the same depth

questions.title: Average insertion cost in a BST
questions.statement: Under the usual random-insertion assumption, what is the average time complexity of inserting an element into an ordinary binary search tree?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0038.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0049.jpg
questions.explanation: Insertion follows a root-to-null search path, taking O(h) for height h. Random insertion order gives logarithmic expected path length. An unbalanced tree built from sorted values can instead have height n and O(n) insertion; a balanced BST guarantees O(log n).
questions.notes: The average-case input assumption is stated explicitly; it is absent from the source.

questions.title: All-or-nothing transaction execution
questions.statement: Which transaction property means either all operations of a transaction occur or none do, with no partial committed transaction?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0039.jpg
questions.explanation: Atomicity is the all-or-nothing guarantee. Consistency preserves declared invariants, isolation governs interactions between concurrent transactions, and durability preserves committed results after failures.

questions.title: Number of tuples in a relation
questions.statement: What is the term for the number of tuples (rows) in a relation?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0040.jpg
questions.explanation: Relation cardinality is its number of tuples. Degree or arity is its number of attributes (columns). An entity is a represented object, not the row-count term.

questions.title: Data Control Language commands
questions.statement: Which listed commands belong to Data Control Language?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0041.jpg
questions.explanation: GRANT assigns privileges and REVOKE removes them. They control access permissions and are conventionally classified as DCL. Their exact privilege and role semantics depend on the database system.

questions.title: Transaction property preserving a bank-transfer invariant
questions.statement: A transaction reads x, subtracts 50 and writes x, then reads y, adds 50 and writes y. Which ACID property describes preserving the constraint that x+y is unchanged?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0042.jpg
questions.explanation: The invariant x+y must be valid before and after a completed transaction: consistency. Isolation can be needed to prevent concurrent operations from violating the invariant, but it is a separate guarantee about interactions. Durability concerns persistence after commit, not the sum itself.

questions.title: Expansion of DBaaS
questions.statement: What does DBaaS stand for?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0043.jpg
questions.explanation: DBaaS means Database as a Service: a provider offers a managed database service rather than requiring the customer to operate the underlying database infrastructure. Management responsibilities still vary by service.

questions.title: Typical effect of a database cache tier
questions.statement: Which statement contradicts the usual goal of a separately scalable cache tier in front of a database?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0045.jpg
questions.explanation: Cache hits answer repeated reads without reaching the database, usually reducing read workload and latency. A separately deployed cache can scale independently. Misses, invalidation and writes still require careful design; the answer describes the normal intended effect rather than a guarantee for every possible workload.
questions.answer: A cache tier increases database workloads
options: A cache tier improves system performance
A cache tier reduces database workloads
A cache tier can be scaled up independently
A cache tier increases database workloads

questions.title: Purpose of NAT
questions.statement: Which listed task describes a common use of Network Address Translation?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0047.jpg
questions.explanation: NAT rewrites IP addresses, often together with transport ports, to allow hosts using private addresses to communicate through public addresses. DNS resolves names; DHCP assigns network configuration; encryption is a different task.
questions.answer: Map private IP addresses to public IP addresses for internet access
options: Translate domain names to IP addresses
Encrypt network traffic for secure communication
Assign IP addresses dynamically to devices
Map private IP addresses to public IP addresses for internet access

questions.title: Day of the week after 62 days
questions.statement: If today is Monday, what day is it after 62 days?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0050.jpg
questions.explanation: 62 leaves remainder 6 when divided by 7. Six days after Monday is Sunday; each complete seven-day block leaves the weekday unchanged.

questions.title: Remainder when 1,992 is divided by 92
questions.statement: What is the remainder when 1,992 is divided by 92?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0053.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\ORACLE-MCQ-Final.pdf
questions.explanation: 92×21=1,932 and 1,992−1,932=60. Since 0≤60<92, the remainder is 60, which is absent from the numeric choices.

questions.title: Find two workers with the same rate
questions.statement: A and B together complete a job in 10 days. B and C together take 5 days. C and D together take 4 days. A alone takes 40 days. Which pair work at the same rate?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0055.jpg
questions.explanation: In jobs per day, a=1/40. Then b=1/10−1/40=3/40, c=1/5−3/40=5/40, and d=1/4−5/40=5/40. Thus C and D each take 8 days alone.

questions.title: Two inscribed angles along a semicircle
questions.statement: A, B, C, D and E are distinct points, in that order, on one semicircular arc. A and E are the endpoints of its diameter. What is ∠ABC + ∠CDE? The source options are 135°, 180°, 225°, 315° and 90°.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0057.jpg
questions.explanation: Let the upper arcs AC and CE have measures u and v. Because AE is a diameter, u+v=180°. Angle ABC intercepts the other arc AC, so it equals (360°−u)/2. Similarly CDE=(360°−v)/2. Their sum is 360°−(u+v)/2=270°. None of the visible options matches the stated geometry. For example equal arc spacing makes both angles 135°, confirming the sum 270°.
questions.notes: The full diagram and point-order statement are visible, but the calculated answer is absent from the source options. No incorrect option is automatically graded.

questions.title: Distance from the starting point after three left turns
questions.statement: A hiker walks 50 m north, turns left and walks 30 m, turns left and walks 50 m, then turns left and walks 50 m. How far is the hiker from the starting point?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0059.jpg
questions.explanation: The north and south legs cancel. The westward 30 m and eastward 50 m leave a displacement of 20 m east, so the distance is 20 m. This is absent from the listed numeric choices.

questions.title: Repeated digit sum of 25 factorial
questions.statement: Repeatedly sum the decimal digits of 25! until one digit remains. What is that digit?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0060.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0062.jpg
questions.explanation: 25! includes enough factors of 3 to be divisible by 9. A positive integer divisible by 9 has digital root 9, since every digit-sum step preserves the residue modulo 9. There is no need to expand the factorial.

questions.title: Expected number of vegetarians in a two-person sample
questions.statement: Of 50 people, 20 are vegetarian. Two people are selected uniformly at random without replacement. What is the expected number of vegetarians selected?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0061.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0063.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0066.jpg
questions.explanation: Each of the two selected positions has probability 20/50 of being vegetarian. By linearity of expectation, the expected count is 2×20/50=4/5=196/245. Independence is not required, so sampling without replacement does not change this expectation.

questions.title: Father and son ages at a vacation
questions.statement: A man spent one-third of his life up to the vacation as a bachelor. His son was born ten years after his marriage. At the vacation, the father was twice as old as his son. How old was the father?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0065.jpg
questions.explanation: Let the father’s vacation age be F. He married at F/3, so the son was born when the father was F/3+10. The son’s age at the vacation is F−(F/3+10)=2F/3−10. Since F=2(2F/3−10), F=60. He married at 20, had his son at 30, and their vacation ages were 60 and 30.

questions.title: Cardinality of a real-valued rational-inequality solution set
questions.statement: S contains all positive real x satisfying (x²+5x+4)/(x²−7x+12) ≤ 0, with x≠3,4. What is the cardinality of S? The source choices are 0, 1, 2 and 3.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0058.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0071.jpg
questions.explanation: Factor the numerator as (x+1)(x+4), which is positive for x>0. The denominator (x−3)(x−4) is negative precisely when 3<x<4. The numerator never vanishes in the positive domain. Hence S=(3,4), an uncountably infinite set, and none of the listed finite counts is correct. If the setter had meant positive integers, there would be no solutions, but that is a different domain.
questions.notes: Both screenshots explicitly say real positive values. The finite MCQ choices do not match that domain.

questions.title: Maximum value sum along any nonempty tree path
questions.statement: A tree rooted at node 0 is given by parent and values arrays. parent[i] identifies the parent of i and parent[0]=−1. Return the maximum sum of node values along any nonempty simple path. The path can start and finish anywhere and need not pass through the root. The tree is not restricted to two children per node.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0072.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0073.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0074.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0075.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\DOC-20240809-WA0022.pdf
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\Final_oracle_coding.pdf
questions.explanation: Process nodes in postorder. For each node, keep the largest downward sum beginning there: its value plus the largest positive child gain, or its value alone. A path whose highest node is this node can use at most two child branches, so update the global answer with the node value plus its two largest positive child gains. Initialise the answer to a node value rather than zero to handle all-negative input. Build an explicit traversal order and process it backwards to avoid Python recursion depth on a 100,000-node chain. O(n) time and O(n) space.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵; parent[0]=−1. Full value bounds are unclear in the angled screenshot.

questions.title: Infer an alleged methodological failure from a passage
questions.statement:
Passage summary: Ancient political writers seriously and systematically organised data about political life and sought rules explaining how regimes arise and disappear. Their alleged failure lay in the way they pursued this study, rather than a lack of effort; later thinkers criticised their methodological naivety.

According to the passage, what were the ancient writers allegedly unsuccessful at?

Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0052.jpg
questions.explanation: The criticism targets their method of inquiry. The passage explicitly acknowledges serious, systematic effort, ruling out insufficient effort and failure to study data systematically. It does not attribute the failure to a particular misunderstanding of how laws arise. The methodology choice best captures the stated criticism.
questions.answer: Establishing a methodology for the study of political science
options: Establishing a methodology for the study of political science
Putting enough effort into establishing the discipline
Understanding how rules and laws came into being and passed away

Bread costs also contributed to unrest, but the passage does not establish a single exclusive cause of the broad political failure. Neither citizens rejecting ideals nor nobles blocking their implementation is explicitly stated. Assess the answer from the given passage.

questions.title: Find a known-lighter coin among nine
questions.statement: There are nine visually identical coins. Exactly one is lighter than the others. What is the minimum number of balance-scale weighings needed in the worst case to find it?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240913-WA0005.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240915-WA0074.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\oracle mcqs.pdf
questions.explanation: Divide the coins into groups of three and weigh two groups. If balanced, the lighter coin is in the unweighed group; otherwise it is in the lighter group. From those three, weigh one against another: the lighter coin is identified either by imbalance or as the third coin if balanced. One weighing has only three outcomes, insufficient to distinguish nine candidates, so two is optimal.

questions.title: Minimum worst-case drops for two eggs and 100 floors
questions.statement: A building has 100 floors. An egg breaks when dropped from floor N or above and survives below N. With two eggs, what minimum worst-case number of drops determines the threshold?

questions.explanation: With d drops and two eggs, the largest searchable floor count is 1+2+…+d=d(d+1)/2. Drop the first egg at floors 14,27,39,…, decreasing the interval by one each time. If it breaks, use the second egg to search the previous interval linearly within the remaining budget. Thirteen drops cover at most 91 floors; fourteen cover 105, enough for 100. The count is a worst-case guarantee.

questions.title: Daily overlaps of clock hands
questions.statement: The hour and minute hands of a regular clock coincide at midnight. How many times do they coincide in a 24-hour day, counting its starting midnight and excluding the next day’s starting midnight?

Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\oracle mcqs.pdf
questions.explanation: The minute hand gains on the hour hand at 6−0.5=5.5 degrees per minute. Consecutive coincidences are 360/5.5=720/11 minutes apart. There are eleven per twelve-hour half-open interval and twenty-two per day. Counting both midnight endpoints would count the shared boundary twice.
questions.notes: The standard day-boundary convention is stated explicitly.

questions.title: Probability three ants do not collide
questions.statement: Three ants start at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Independently, each chooses clockwise or counterclockwise with equal probability and moves along its edges at the same speed. What is the probability that no ants collide?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240913-WA0012.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240915-WA0071.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\oracle mcqs.pdf
questions.explanation: There are 2³=8 equally likely direction assignments. Collision is avoided only when all three go clockwise or all three go counterclockwise, giving 2/8=1/4. Mixed directions cause at least one pair to approach along the same edge.
questions.notes: Independent fair direction choices and equal speed make the usual puzzle assumptions explicit.

questions.title: Recover the first two terms of a multiplicative sequence
questions.statement: A sequence has 100 real elements. Every element except the first and last equals the product of its two neighbours. The product of the first 50 elements is 27, and the product of all 100 is also 27. Find the sum of the first two elements.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240913-WA0004.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240913-WA0013.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240915-WA0080.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\oracle mcqs.pdf
questions.explanation: All elements are nonzero because their total product is 27. Writing the first two as a,b, the recurrence gives the repeating six-term cycle a,b,b/a,1/a,1/b,a/b, whose product is 1. Fifty terms comprise eight cycles followed by a,b, so ab=27. A hundred terms comprise sixteen cycles followed by a,b,b/a,1/a, so b²/a=27. Substituting a=27/b gives b³=729, hence b=9, a=3 and a+b=12.

questions.title: TCP delivery ordering and acknowledgement
questions.statement: Which mechanism lets TCP track ordered delivery and identify data that has been received?

questions.explanation: TCP numbers bytes in the stream and acknowledges received data. The receiver can reorder segments, detect gaps and reject duplicate data; retransmission can recover missing segments. Checksums help detect corruption. A connection handshake establishes the connection but does not by itself provide the ongoing delivery tracking.

questions.title: BGP name and position above its transport
questions.statement: What does BGP stand for, and which layer contains its messages when classifying the protocol by its use of TCP as transport?

Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\oracle mcqs.pdf
questions.explanation: BGP is Border Gateway Protocol. Its messages run over TCP, using port 179, so this encapsulation-based classification puts BGP above transport at the application layer. Its purpose is to exchange network-layer reachability information; that routing function should not be confused with how its own messages are transported. See [RFC 4271](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4271.html).

questions.title: Binary versus two-permit semaphore around updates
questions.statement: X starts at 10. Five threads each execute wait(S); X=X+1; signal(S), and three execute wait(S); X=X−1; signal(S). Compare the minimum final values with (1) a binary semaphore initially 1 and (2) a counting semaphore initially 2. The source options are (15,7), (7,7), (12,7), (12,8).

questions.explanation: Under the usual abstract model where each assignment has separately atomic read and write steps, the answer is (12,7). One permit gives mutual exclusion, preserving all updates: 10+5−3=12. Two permits allow lost updates. One decrement can read 10 and pause; all five increments run using the other permit; that pending decrement then writes 9, discarding their effects. The two remaining decrements reduce it to 7. Fewer than 7 is impossible with only three decrement operations. If this were implemented in C/C++ using an ordinary shared variable, allowing concurrent unsynchronised updates creates a data race instead of a well-defined numeric outcome; use a mutex or atomic operations.
questions.notes: The read/write model is not specified in the source. The explanation makes the exam-style interleaving assumption explicit, without a portable-code guarantee.

questions.title: Count partitions with alternating odd/even segment sums
questions.statement: Partition a positive integer array into one or more nonempty contiguous segments covering every element exactly once. Adjacent segment sums must have opposite parity. Count the different valid partitions modulo 10⁹+7. A one-segment partition is always valid.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240914-WA0065.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240914-WA0066.jpg

Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240914-WA0068.jpg
questions.explanation: Let P[i] be the parity of the prefix ending at i, with P[0]=0. For a previous cut j, the last segment parity is P[i] XOR P[j]. Maintain four sums B[prefix parity][previous last-segment parity] over already processed nonempty prefixes. For current parity t, ways ending even are B[t][1] plus 1 if t=0; ways ending odd are B[t XOR 1][0] plus 1 if t=1. The added 1 represents taking the whole prefix as a single segment. Compute both values before inserting them into B[t], so no zero-length segment is counted. Sum the two values at the final index, reducing all accumulators modulo 10⁹+7. O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

examples.explanation: Either one segment, or segments [1], [1,1], [1].

Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\Final_oracle_coding.pdf
questions.explanation: The objective is one-dimensional minimax k-centre, not ordinary k-means (which minimises squared-distance sum). Sort the points and binary-search a coverage width D. Greedily start each interval at the leftmost uncovered point and include every point at most D farther right; D is feasible when at most k intervals suffice. This placement covers as far right as any feasible interval containing that leftmost point. With unrestricted real centres, a span D can be covered at its midpoint with radius D/2. The minimum feasible D is an integer for integer input. The sample locations [1,9,3,10,14], k=2 have optimal real radius 2.5, yet the source returns 3; its integer outputs fit ceiling the radius or requiring integer centres. Clarify that policy before implementing a judge. The integer-radius variant tests width 2R and returns the smallest feasible R. O(n log n+n log W) time and O(n) sorted-copy space, where W is the coordinate range.

examples.explanation: Centres 2 and 11.5 achieve a real radius of 2.5; the source instead shows centres 3 and 12.

questions.notes: Centre-coordinate/rounding semantics are inconsistent between the continuous wording and integer samples. No practice checker is attached.

questions.title: Review incomplete range-partition DDL
questions.statement: An orders table needs order_id (primary key), customer_id, order_date and total_amount. The source offers fragments beginning with CREATE TABLE orders, then a PARTITION BY RANGE clause, but omits all column declarations. One fragment uses RANGE COLUMNS; another appends PRIMARY KEY(order_id) after the partitions. Can any be accepted as a complete Oracle CREATE TABLE statement? Show a complete range-partitioned form.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240730-WA0069.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240823-WA0106.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\ORACLE-MCQ-Final.pdf
questions.explanation:
None of the displayed fragments is a complete Oracle table definition: the column declarations are missing. Oracle uses PARTITION BY RANGE (order_date), not the shown RANGE COLUMNS form. Define the primary key within the table definition and use explicit DATE literals for date bounds. A complete illustration is:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id NUMBER,
  order_date DATE,
  total_amount NUMBER(12,2)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (order_date) (
  PARTITION p1 VALUES LESS THAN (DATE '2023-01-01'),
  PARTITION p2 VALUES LESS THAN (DATE '2024-01-01'),
  PARTITION p_future VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE)
);
```

The final partition accommodates later dates; the first two bounds are exclusive. Data types and the final partition are supplied for this illustration, not recovered from the options. The source’s tentative “C (maybe)” is not a verified answer. See [Oracle CREATE TABLE](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/sqlrf/CREATE-TABLE.html).
questions.notes: The source does not name a dialect; the discussion explicitly uses Oracle SQL. The original options are incomplete and are not automatically graded.

questions.title: Animal survival probabilities versus family composition
questions.statement: There are 729 farmers, each owning six animals that are cows or hens. A flood occurs. A hen survives with probability 1/3 and a cow with probability 2/3. The source asks how many families have two hens and four cows. Does the supplied information determine that count?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240913-WA0048.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\IMG-20240915-WA0088.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\oracle mcqs.pdf
questions.explanation: No. Species-specific survival probabilities do not give the initial animal composition, independence between outcomes or an observed number of survivors. The actual family count is therefore not determined. A different binomial model, in which each of six independent positions is a hen with probability 1/3 and a cow with probability 2/3, gives expected count 729×C(6,2)×(1/3)²×(2/3)⁴=240. That is a conditional expectation under an added composition model, not a consequence of the photographed survival statement and not a guaranteed realised count.
questions.notes: The source’s species/survival wording is retained as an ambiguity; its numerical options are not automatically graded.

questions.title: Maximum sum along a downward tree path
questions.statement: Reconstructed from a solution-only collection: Given a nonempty rooted tree described by parent and values arrays, find the largest node-value sum along a nonempty downward path. It may begin at any node and end at a descendant, but every edge must move from parent to child. The unique root has parent −1.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Oracle\Final_oracle_coding.pdf
questions.explanation: Visit parents before children. Let best_end[u] be the largest sum of a downward path ending at u. At the root it equals values[u]; elsewhere it is values[u]+max(0,best_end[parent[u]]). The answer is the largest best_end value. Initialise from a node value to handle all-negative trees. Build child lists and traverse iteratively rather than assuming parent indices precede their children or recursing down a deep chain. O(n) time and O(n) space. Unlike an unrestricted simple tree path, a downward path cannot join two child branches through their parent.
questions.constraints: Arrays have equal positive length and describe a valid rooted tree. Original OA size/value bounds are not included in this solution-only source.

examples.explanation: The downward path 1→2 gives 10+10; joining node 4 would require an upward edge.

questions.notes: This problem definition is reconstructed from the titled implementation, not a verbatim OA statement. No official judge constraints or tests are available.

questions.title: Maximum quality of a machine cluster
questions.statement: Each machine has a positive integer speed and reliability. Select a nonempty cluster containing at most maxMachines machines. Its quality is the sum of selected speeds multiplied by the minimum selected reliability. Return the maximum possible quality, without applying a modulus.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\BNY Melon\IMG-20240820-WA0103.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\BNY Melon\IMG-20240820-WA0104.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\BNY Melon\IMG-20240820-WA0105.jpg
questions.explanation: Sort machines by decreasing reliability. Maintain a min-heap of at most maxMachines speeds and their sum. Insert the current speed, discarding the smallest if the heap is too large, and consider speed_sum×current_reliability. At an optimal cluster’s minimum reliability, all its machines have become eligible; retaining the largest eligible speeds maximises the sum for that threshold. Evaluate all thresholds, not only clusters of exactly maxMachines machines: fewer machines can be better. O(n log n+n log k) time and O(n+k) space with the sorted list. Products can exceed a 32-bit integer; use Python integers or a wide type. [LeetCode 1383](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-performance-of-a-team/) uses the same optimisation but requires a modulus, which this source does not.

examples.explanation: The third machine alone is optimal.

questions.title: Remove leaves to eliminate ancestor-distance violations
questions.statement: A weighted undirected tree is rooted at node 1. Each node y has a positive limit arr[y]. The remaining tree must have no ancestor x and descendant y for which the sum of edge weights on x→y exceeds arr[y]. Repeatedly remove a current leaf, keeping the root. Return the minimum total number of removed nodes; each deletion is one leaf-removal operation. Edge weights may be negative.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\BNY Melon\IMG-20240820-WA0106.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\BNY Melon\IMG-20240820-WA0107.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\BNY Melon\IMG-20240820-WA0108.jpg
questions.explanation: For each node y, compute the largest ancestor-to-y path sum, including the zero-length path. Starting with d[root]=0, an edge of weight w from x to y gives d[y]=max(0,d[x]+w). If d[y]>arr[y], y must be removed; to delete it as a leaf, every descendant must be removed first, so remove its whole subtree. Otherwise continue to its children. Count all nodes beneath the first violating ancestor. An iterative DFS carrying distance and a removed flag handles deep trees in O(n) time and O(n) space. With negative weights, root distance alone is insufficient: the largest suffix can begin at a later ancestor. Equality is permitted by the stated “no arr[y]<distance” condition. [Codeforces 682C](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/682/C) has the same pruning pattern.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ tree_nodes ≤ 10⁵; tree_edges=tree_nodes−1; connected tree; arr values are positive. Exact weight bounds are blurred in the source.

examples.explanation: Remove leaves 2 and 5.

questions.notes: The source’s existential “a pair” phrasing conflicts with its “no instance” condition and worked example. The cleaned prompt uses the universal no-violation interpretation supported by the example; its explanation uses > comparisons even though the condition allows equality.

questions.title: Minimise the largest adjacent-value jump along a path
questions.statement: An undirected graph has N nodes, M edges and an integer value A[i] at each node. A path’s value is the maximum absolute difference |A[u]−A[v]| across its edges. Given start S and end E, return the minimum possible path value.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zepto\IMG-20240804-WA0120.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zepto\IMG-20240804-WA0121.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zepto\IMG-20240804-WA0122.jpg
questions.explanation: Treat each edge (u,v) as having weight |A[u]−A[v]|. Use Dijkstra’s algorithm with bottleneck distance: initialise dist[S]=0 and relax an edge with candidate=max(dist[u],edge_weight), taking the smaller candidate at v. Pop the smallest candidate from a min-heap and discard stale entries; the first settled destination gives the optimum. Alternatively sort edges by weight and union endpoints until S and E are connected. Heap Dijkstra is O((N+M) log(N+M)) time with lazy heap entries and O(N+M) space. A sum-of-weights shortest path optimises a different objective.
questions.function_signature: pathValue(N, M, S, E, edge, A)
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 10⁵; N−1 ≤ M ≤ 10⁶; 1 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10⁶. The photos do not specify the unreachable-case return value or the zero-edge S=E case.

examples.explanation: The path 2→3→1→5 has differences 2,1,1.

questions.notes: Do not infer connectivity merely from M≥N−1. Clarify missing endpoint/failure conventions before attaching a judge.

questions.title: Tree paths whose edge labels can form a palindrome
questions.statement: A tree has g_nodes vertices numbered 1 through g_nodes. Each edge has a label in 1…26 representing A…Z. Count unordered pairs of distinct vertices whose unique path has edge characters that can be rearranged into a palindrome.
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\ThoughtSpot\IMG-20241105-WA0001.jpg
oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\ThoughtSpot\IMG-20241105-WA0004.jpg
questions.explanation: Assign each node a 26-bit root-path parity mask: toggle the bit of each traversed edge label. The XOR of two node masks gives odd/even edge-label counts on their connecting path. Rearrangement into a palindrome is possible exactly when this XOR has zero or one set bit. Process masks one at a time: add the stored frequency of the same mask and of each of its 26 single-bit neighbours, then increment this mask’s frequency. This counts each unordered distinct pair once and excludes self-pairs. Iterative traversal avoids depth limits. O(26n) time and O(n) space. Use a wide count because n(n−1)/2 can exceed signed 32-bit range.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ g_nodes ≤ 10⁵; g_edges=g_nodes−1; 1 ≤ edge labels ≤ 26; the reported tree diameter is less than 1000.

questions.title: Count numbers without repeated digits in inclusive ranges
questions.statement: For each inclusive integer range [n,m], print the number of integers whose usual decimal representation has no repeated digit. Ranges may contain up to one million, and there may be up to 100,000 queries.
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\ThoughtSpot\IMG-20241105-WA0002.jpg
oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\ThoughtSpot\IMG-20241105-WA0005.jpg
questions.explanation: Precompute a prefix count through the largest queried endpoint B. Check each integer with a ten-bit digit mask; a previously set bit means a repeated digit. Leading zeros are not part of the usual representation. Set prefix[x]=prefix[x−1]+valid(x), then answer [n,m] as prefix[m]−prefix[n−1]. O(B log B+q) time and O(B) space. Alternatively digit DP answers counts up to each bound without enumerating B, useful for larger domains.

examples.explanation: There are 41 integers in the range; 14 repeat a digit.

questions.title: Count distinct sums of two integer powers
questions.statement: Count integers x in the inclusive range [l,r] that can be written as a^p+b^q, where a,b are nonnegative integers and p,q are integers greater than 1. Count x once even when it has multiple representations.
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\ThoughtSpot\IMG-20241105-WA0003.jpg
questions.explanation: Generate a set P of all power values at most r. Include 0 and, if r≥1, 1. For each base from 2 through floor(sqrt(r)), repeatedly multiply starting at its square while the value is ≤r. Deduplicate before pairing. Sort P and enumerate unordered pairs of power values, allowing the same value twice; mark each sum ≤r in a byte array and stop a row when sums exceed r. Count marked entries in [l,r]. If t=|P|, this straightforward method takes O(r+t²+sqrt(r) log r) time and O(r+t) space. Deduplicating sums is essential: the problem counts integers, not base/exponent tuples. For r=0, 0=0²+0² is valid.

questions.title: Minimum grid jumps with a forced next direction
questions.statement: A grid uses * for empty cells, # for blocked cells, S for the start and E for the destination. Jump any positive integer distance horizontally or vertically; intermediate blocked cells may be crossed but the landing cell must be traversable. After a jump of length greater than one, the next jump must use the same direction. A length-one jump frees the direction for the following jump. The final jump must have length one. Return the minimum number of jumps from S to E, or −1 if impossible.
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\ThoughtSpot\WhatsApp Image 2024-11-05 at 02.30.10_ea0f0e3b.jpg
questions.explanation: Run BFS over (row,column,direction_state). State FREE permits four directions; after a long jump the state forces its direction until a length-one jump resets it to FREE. Each legal jump is one edge regardless of length. Enumerate positive lengths up to the grid boundary and skip blocked landing cells without stopping the ray. Accept the destination only in FREE state, ensuring the final jump had length one; reaching E after a long jump does not finish the route. Five states per cell use O(nm) space. Direct ray enumeration costs O(nm(n+m)) time. For larger grids, maintain unvisited forced-state landing positions in ordered row/column sets and remove a destination after first discovery, while handling length-one moves separately; this avoids repeatedly scanning the same long-jump targets. The source omits grid-size bounds, so select the implementation after clarifying them.
questions.constraints: Exactly one S and one E; full dimension bounds and the original function signature are not shown.

questions.title: Smallest integer-coordinate square strictly containing k points
questions.statement: Given integer point coordinates x[i],y[i], find the minimum area of an axis-aligned square with integer-coordinate vertices that contains at least k points strictly inside. Points on a square’s boundary do not count.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Visa\IMG-20240831-WA0055.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Visa\IMG-20240831-WA0056.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Visa\IMG-20240831-WA0057.jpg
questions.explanation: Enumerate the leftmost and rightmost point x-coordinates of a candidate subset. Collect y-coordinates of all points in that inclusive x-band and sort them. For every window of k consecutive y-values, let span_y be its last minus first value and span_x the x-band width. These k points fit strictly inside an integer-vertex square of side max(span_x,span_y)+2: integer boundaries must lie at least one unit beyond each extreme. Minimise the squared side over all bands and windows. Considering the actual x-extremes of an optimal k-point subset ensures it is represented. O(n³ log n) time and O(n) extra space with n≤100. The +2 is essential; even a single point needs side 2 and area 4. Use wide arithmetic for coordinates near ±10⁹.

examples.explanation: The square from (0,0) to (3,3) contains all points strictly inside.

questions.notes: The source says integer coordinates and its side-3 example supports integer square vertices; permitting arbitrary real vertices would yield a different infimum.

questions.title: Minimum cost to balance two lines of student heights
questions.statement: Two arrays arrA and arrB each contain n positive student heights. Rearranging within a line is free. Swapping a student from A with one from B costs the smaller of their two heights. Find the minimum total swap cost that makes the two height multisets equal, or −1 if impossible.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Atlassian\6303073255631731816.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Atlassian\6303073255631731817.jpg

questions.explanation: Count each height in the combined arrays. If any combined count is odd, equality is impossible. Let d[h]=countA[h]−countB[h]; A must export d[h]/2 copies when d[h]>0, and B must export −d[h]/2 copies when d[h]<0. All differences must be even, including negative ones. Build the two excess lists, sort one ascending and the other descending, and pair them. For each pair (a,b), pay min(a,b,2g), where g is the global minimum height across both arrays. The 2g route swaps through g twice and restores g to its original line while exchanging a and b. Pairing opposite orders gives the cheapest direct minima; the same 2g cap applies independently to every exchange. Sum costs using a wide integer. O(n log n) time and O(n) space. [LeetCode 2561](https://leetcode.com/problems/rearranging-fruits/) has the same cost model.

examples.explanation: Swap a 2 in A with a 1 in B.

questions.title: Order meetings to keep a positive effectiveness index
questions.statement: A manager begins with effectiveness index zero. Each meeting changes it by the given signed effectiveness value. Rearrange the meetings to maximise how many can be held while the running index stays strictly greater than zero after every held meeting. Return that maximum number.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\linkedin oa\IMG-20240801-WA0025.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\linkedin oa\IMG-20240801-WA0027.jpg
questions.explanation: Sort effectiveness in decreasing order and accumulate. Count meetings until the next cumulative sum is zero or negative. The largest k values have the greatest possible sum of any k meetings, so no other order can make a length-k prefix positive if the descending prefix is nonpositive. Descending order also keeps earlier sums as large as possible. Once a descending prefix fails, its latest contribution is nonpositive and all later contributions are no larger, so recovery cannot occur. Strict positivity means a zero sum does not count. O(n log n) time and O(n) space for a sorted copy; use a wide running sum.

questions.title: Minimum population-weighted Manhattan travel cost
questions.statement: City i is at integer coordinates (x[i],y[i]) and has numPeople[i] residents. A festival can be located at any integer point (a,b). Every resident attends and pays |x[i]−a|+|y[i]−b|. Return the minimum total travel cost over all locations.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\linkedin oa\IMG-20240801-WA0026.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\linkedin oa\IMG-20240801-WA0028.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\linkedin oa\IMG-20240801-WA0029.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\linkedin oa\IMG-20240801-WA0030.jpg
questions.explanation: The x and y terms separate. For each coordinate axis, sort cities by that coordinate, accumulate their populations and select the first coordinate where twice the cumulative population is at least the total. This is a weighted median. Place the festival at the independently chosen x and y weighted medians and sum each city’s population times its Manhattan distance. Moving across a coordinate changes the slope by twice the population there; a median balances weight on both sides. Do not use an unweighted median or arithmetic mean. O(n log n) time and O(n) space. When the total population is split equally, an interval of integer coordinates can be optimal; any weighted median endpoint suffices.

examples.explanation: Hold it at (3,3).
Any location (a,1) with a in {1,2,3} is optimal.

questions.notes: The second source example lists optimal coordinates in reversed order; the cleaned example follows the stated x/y arrays and Manhattan formula.

questions.explanation: Sort each player’s triple as (a,b,c). X can beat Y exactly when b_X>a_Y and c_X>b_Y: pair X’s two largest boosters against Y’s two smallest and sacrifice the remaining round. These inequalities are also necessary for matching two distinct winning comparisons. Thus player i qualifies when its middle booster exceeds the largest smallest-booster value among other players, and its largest exceeds the largest middle-booster value among other players. Track the top two entries for each of those opponent statistics, including ties and their player indices, so excluding i still gives the true other-player maximum. Sorting triples is constant work; bounded top-two updates and one final pass take O(n) time and O(n) space for stored triples. This is existential pairwise capability: multiple players can qualify; it is not a guaranteed strategy against every simultaneous hidden ordering.
questions.constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵; booster values are 1…10⁹; each player’s three values are distinct.

questions.title: Count product pairs with a sum divisible by x
questions.statement: Given positive integer product costs, count index pairs i<j for which cost[i]+cost[j] is divisible by the positive integer x. Equal costs at different indices remain different products.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\amazon\IMG-20240914-WA0069.jpg

questions.explanation: Scan once with a frequency dictionary of seen remainders. For a new remainder r=cost% x, add the number of earlier products with remainder (−r)%x, then increment frequency[r]. Updating after counting excludes self-pairs and counts each unordered index pair once. A dictionary handles x as large as 2×10⁹ without allocating x slots. Expected O(n) time and O(min(n,x)) space. questions.title: Minimum total fare after halving with at most X coupons
questions.statement: Adarsh wants to take $N$ Uber trips; the fare of trip $i$ is $A_i$ rupees. He has $X$ coupons. Each coupon halves the fare of a trip using floor division ($A_i \to \lfloor A_i/2 \rfloor$). Any number of coupons (at most $X$ in total) may be used on one trip. Find the minimum total amount needed to take every trip.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\uber oa\IMG-20240721-WA0058.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\uber oa\IMG-20240721-WA0059.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\uber oa\IMG-20240721-WA0060.jpg
questions.explanation: Each coupon removes ceil(a/2) from a fare a, and that gain only grows with a. So the best use of a coupon is always on the currently largest fare. Keep a max-heap, apply X halvings to the top, stop early if the top becomes 0. O((N+X) log N).
questions.function_signature: long long solution(int n, int x, vector<long long> cost)
questions.input_format: N, X, then N fares.
questions.output_format: The minimum total fare.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ N, X ≤ 10⁵; 1 ≤ A_i ≤ 10⁹; time limit 0.5 s.

examples.explanation: Apply both coupons to 128: 128 -> 64 -> 32, giving [1, 2, 4, 32] with total 39.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
A coupon saves ceil(a/2) on a fare a. Savings are bigger on bigger fares, so every coupon should go to whichever fare is largest right now.

### Approach
1. Put all fares in a max-heap (negate values in Python).
2. Repeat X times: look at the maximum; if it is 0, stop; otherwise replace it by floor(max/2).
3. Answer is the sum of the heap.

### Why it works
Exchange argument: the saving from halving a fare a is a - floor(a/2) = ceil(a/2), which is non-decreasing in a, and after a halving the same fare offers a smaller next saving. So the multiset of available savings is "decreasing per fare", and picking the X largest available savings greedily (which the heap does) is optimal. Any plan that gives a coupon to a smaller fare while a larger one exists can be improved by swapping that coupon.

### Complexity
O((N + X) log N) time (each pop/push is log N, and X ≤ 10⁵), O(N) space.

### Python solution
```python
import heapq


def min_total_fare(n, x, cost):
    heap = [-c for c in cost]          # max-heap via negation
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    for _ in range(x):
        top = -heap[0]
        if top == 0:                    # nothing left to reduce
            break
        heapq.heapreplace(heap, -(top // 2))
    return -sum(heap)
```

### Dry run
Fares [1,2,4,128], X=2: heap top 128 -> 64, then top 64 -> 32. Fares are now [1,2,4,32]; the sum is 39.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Stop early once the maximum is 0 (fares of 1 become 0 after one coupon; further coupons do nothing).
- Use 64-bit sums: N·A can reach 10¹⁴.
- X can exceed the useful number of halvings (each fare halves to 0 in about 30 steps); the early exit handles it.
- Floor division, not true halving: 5 becomes 2.

questions.title: Recover distance and time from four mixed-up derived values
questions.statement:
Uber stores derived values instead of distance and time: uSpeed = floor(Distance / Time), uAlpha = Time + Distance, uBeta = Time × Distance and uDelta = Time − Distance. The four values got shuffled and it is not known which is which. For each test case, return the Distance followed by the Time. Assume the absolute value of the distance is always greater than the time. If no such integers exist, return -1, -1.

For example, Time = 10 and Distance = 12 gives uSpeed = 1, uAlpha = 22, uBeta = 120, uDelta = -2, so an input record can be [-2, 1, 22, 120].
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\uber oa\IMG-20240721-WA0062.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\uber oa\IMG-20240721-WA0063.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\uber oa\IMG-20240721-WA0064.jpg
questions.explanation: Try the 24 assignments of the four numbers to (speed, alpha, beta, delta). Alpha and delta give d = (alpha - delta)/2 and t = (alpha + delta)/2; they must be integers (equal parity), t is non-zero and |d| > |t|. Accept the assignment if d·t equals beta and floor(d/t) equals speed. O(24) per test.
questions.input_format: T test cases, each with four integers A, B, C, D (the mixed-up values).
questions.output_format: For each test case: Distance then Time, or -1 -1 if impossible.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ T ≤ 100000; -10⁹ ≤ A, B, C, D ≤ 10⁹; time limit 0.5 s.

examples.explanation: Time = 10, Distance = 12 as described above.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Alpha = d + t and delta = t - d are two linear equations in d and t. Once we know which input is alpha and which is delta, d and t follow immediately, and the other two numbers are only used to check consistency.

### Approach
1. Enumerate every permutation of the four values as (speed, alpha, beta, delta).
2. Compute d = (alpha - delta)/2 and t = (alpha + delta)/2; skip if either division is not exact.
3. Skip if t = 0 or |d| <= |t| (the problem guarantees |d| > |t|).
4. Check d·t = beta and floor(d/t) = speed. The first assignment passing all checks is the answer; otherwise answer [-1, -1].

### Why it works
Alpha and delta uniquely determine (d, t), and beta and speed are fully determined by (d, t). So a candidate assignment is correct exactly when all four stated relations hold. Trying all 24 permutations covers every possible labelling.

### Complexity
O(24) = O(1) per test case, so O(T) overall; O(1) extra space. Python integers avoid overflow of d·t (up to about 10¹⁸).

### Python solution
```python
from itertools import permutations


def recover(values):
    """values = [A, B, C, D], a mix of speed, alpha (d+t), beta (d*t), delta (t-d).
    Returns [distance, time] or [-1, -1]."""
    for speed, alpha, beta, delta in permutations(values):
        if (alpha - delta) % 2 or (alpha + delta) % 2:
            continue
        d = (alpha - delta) // 2       # alpha - delta = 2d
        t = (alpha + delta) // 2       # alpha + delta = 2t
        if t == 0 or abs(d) <= abs(t):
            continue
        if d * t == beta and d // t == speed:
            return [d, t]
    return [-1, -1]
```

### Dry run
Values [-2, 1, 22, 120]. The permutation speed=1, alpha=22, beta=120, delta=-2 gives d = (22+2)/2 = 12, t = (22-2)/2 = 10; |12| > |10|, 12·10 = 120 and floor(12/10) = 1, so the answer is [12, 10].

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Check parity before dividing: alpha - delta must be even.
- Guard t = 0 before computing floor(d/t).
- Use floor (not truncation) if negative values can occur; Python // does this.
- In C++ use 64-bit for d·t.
questions.notes: Only one worked example is visible. How ties between several valid assignments should be broken, and how floor behaves for negative operands, is not stated; the solution assumes mathematical floor and returns the first valid assignment.

questions.explanation: Equivalence is the transitive closure of "shares a letter", so OTPs fall into connected groups, and one attempt per group is both necessary and sufficient. Union the letters of each OTP in a 26-node DSU and count the distinct roots among the OTPs. O(total length) time.
questions.input_format: n, then n strings.
questions.output_format: An integer: minimum number of OTPs to try.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴; each OTP has lowercase letters only and length at most 50; time limit 0.5 s.

examples.explanation: "a", "b" and "ab" are equivalent; "d" is isolated.
Only one OTP, so it must be tried.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Build a graph whose vertices are OTPs and whose edges join OTPs sharing a letter. "Equivalent" is then "in the same connected component", and trying one OTP per component is the minimum.

### Approach
1. Create a DSU over the 26 letters.
2. For each OTP, union every letter of the OTP with its first letter.
3. Two OTPs are in the same component exactly when their first letters have the same DSU root.
4. Count the distinct roots of the first letters of all OTPs.

### Why it works
If two OTPs share a letter they share a DSU set. If A-C and C-B share letters, then A, C and B all land in one set through the letters of C. Conversely, one set can only be formed by chains of shared letters. So DSU components of letters correspond one-to-one with components of OTPs, and any one OTP of a component is equivalent to all the others.

### Complexity
O(sum of lengths · α(26)) time, about 5·10⁵ operations; O(26) extra space for the DSU.

### Python solution
```python
def min_otps(n, otps):
    parent = list(range(26))

    def find(a):
        while parent[a] != a:
            parent[a] = parent[parent[a]]
            a = parent[a]
        return a

    for s in otps:
        first = ord(s[0]) - 97
        for ch in s:
            ra, rb = find(first), find(ord(ch) - 97)
            if ra != rb:
                parent[ra] = rb
    # number of distinct letter-components that appear in some OTP
    return len({find(ord(s[0]) - 97) for s in otps})
```

### Dry run
["a","b","ab","d"]: "a" has only a; "b" only b; "ab" unions a and b; "d" alone. Roots of first letters: a and b share a root, d has its own, so 2 components.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Do not count letters that appear in no OTP.
- Duplicate OTPs are allowed and fall in the same component.
- A single OTP gives 1.
- Comparing every pair of strings is O(n²) and unnecessary.

questions.statement: Uber is partnered with $N$ drivers numbered $1..N$. For each pair $(i, j)$ their similarity is an integer $S_{i,j}$ with $S_{i,j} = S_{j,i}$ and $S_{i,i} = 0$. Uber divides the drivers into any number of teams; each driver is in exactly one team. For every pair $i < j$ in the same team, Uber reduces its efforts by $S_{i,j}$ points. Find the maximum possible total effort Uber can reduce. A team may be of any size.

questions.explanation: Because N ≤ 16, run a subset DP: gain[mask] is the sum of S over pairs inside mask, dp[mask] is the best partition value of mask. For dp[mask], force the lowest set driver into the team and enumerate the submasks of the rest. Total cost is O(3^N).
questions.function_signature: long long solution(int n, vector<vector<int>> s)
questions.input_format: N, then the N×N symmetric similarity matrix.
questions.output_format: The maximum total reduction (64-bit).
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 16; |S[i][j]| up to about 10⁹ (the exponent is partly cropped); S[i][i] = 0; S[i][j] = S[j][i]; time limit 2 s.

examples.explanation: Teams {1,3} and {2}.
One team {1,2,3,4}: 5 pairs of 10 and one pair of -1.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
This is "set partition" with a pairwise score. A team of size k contributes the sum of all its C(k,2) pair similarities. With N ≤ 16 we can afford to try all subsets of subsets.

### Approach
1. gain[mask] = sum of S[i][j] for all pairs i<j inside mask (built incrementally from the mask without its lowest bit).
2. dp[0] = 0. For dp[mask]: let low be the lowest set bit. Enumerate every submask sub of mask without low; the team is sub | low.
3. dp[mask] = max over these teams of gain[team] + dp[mask ^ team].
4. Answer dp[full].

### Why it works
Every partition has exactly one team containing the lowest driver of the current mask, so forcing it into the chosen team enumerates each partition once and does not miss any. The remaining drivers are an independent subproblem because the score is a sum over pairs within teams only.

### Complexity
O(3^N) for the submask enumeration (about 4.3·10⁷ for N = 16) plus O(2^N · N) for gain; O(2^N) memory. In Python the full 3^16 loop is slow; the same algorithm in C++ meets the 2 s limit.

### Python solution
```python
def max_effort(n, s):
    full = (1 << n) - 1
    # gain[mask] = sum of s[i][j] over pairs i<j inside mask
    gain = [0] * (1 << n)
    for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
        low = (mask & -mask).bit_length() - 1
        rest = mask & (mask - 1)
        g = gain[rest]
        m = rest
        while m:
            j = (m & -m).bit_length() - 1
            g += s[low][j]
            m &= m - 1
        gain[mask] = g
    NEG = float('-inf')
    dp = [NEG] * (1 << n)
    dp[0] = 0
    for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
        low = mask & -mask               # the lowest driver must be in some team
        rest = mask ^ low
        sub = rest
        best = NEG
        while True:
            team = sub | low
            v = gain[team] + dp[mask ^ team]
            if v > best:
                best = v
            if sub == 0:
                break
            sub = (sub - 1) & rest
        dp[mask] = best
    return dp[full]
```

### Dry run
Example 1: gain[{1,3}] = 8, gain[{1,2}] = 5, gain[{2,3}] = -10, gain[{1,2,3}] = 3. dp[{1,2,3}] = max(gain[{1}] + dp[{2,3}] = 0 + 0, gain[{1,2}] + dp[{3}] = 5, gain[{1,3}] + dp[{2}] = 8, gain[{1,2,3}] = 3) = 8.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Negative similarities: splitting teams is sometimes better, so never assume one big team.
- Initialise dp with -infinity and always include the "alone" option via sub = 0.
- Use 64-bit values (a team of 16 can sum 120 values of ±10⁹).
- Enumerate submasks of rest = mask ^ low, not of mask, to avoid counting each partition many times.

questions.explanation: Track next = the largest size not yet placed. After brick arr[i] arrives, keep placing next, next-1, ... while that size has already arrived. Each brick is placed once, so O(N) total.
questions.input_format: N, then N integers: the brick size supplied each day.
questions.output_format: N lists, the i-th being the bricks placed on day i in descending order.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 100000; 1 ≤ size ≤ N; all sizes distinct; time limit 1 s.

examples.explanation: Day 2: 5 has arrived so 5 and 4 can be placed. Days 3-4: 3 has not arrived. Day 5: 3, 2, 1.
Placed on the day it arrives.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
The tower must be built strictly in order N, N-1, ..., 1. A brick can only be used once every larger brick is already on the tower, so we are only waiting for the next needed size to show up.

### Approach
1. Keep need = N and a boolean array arrived[].
2. On day i mark arr[i] as arrived and start an empty list for the day.
3. While need >= 1 and arrived[need]: append need to today and decrement need.
4. Record the list for that day (possibly empty).

### Why it works
The set of placed bricks is always {need+1..N}. A brick can be placed exactly when all larger ones are placed and it has arrived, which is the loop condition. Each day we place the maximal run, so nothing placeable is delayed.

### Complexity
O(N) time since need only decreases and each brick is appended once; O(N) space.

### Python solution
```python
def tower_days(n, arr):
    arrived = [False] * (n + 2)
    need = n                        # the largest brick not yet placed
    out = []
    for size in arr:
        arrived[size] = True
        today = []
        while need >= 1 and arrived[need]:
            today.append(need)
            need -= 1
        out.append(today)
    return out
```

### Dry run
arr = [4,5,1,2,3], need = 5. Day 1: 4 arrives, 5 has not -> []. Day 2: 5 arrives -> place 5, 4 (4 already here), need = 3 -> [5,4]. Days 3-4: 1 and 2 arrive but 3 is missing -> []. Day 5: 3 arrives -> place 3, 2, 1 -> [3,2,1].

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Empty days must still print an empty line.
- The sorted-set approach in the screenshot also works, but the boolean array is simpler and O(N).
- Bricks are a permutation of 1..N, so need never goes below 0 incorrectly.
questions.notes: This is the well-known "building a tower of disks" simulation.
