questions.title: Time complexity of linear search
questions.statement: Determine the time complexity of linear search in an array of size n.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0226.jpg
questions.explanation: Linear search inspects elements one by one; in the worst case it examines all n.
questions.solution:
### Solution
In the worst case (key absent or at the last position) the loop compares n elements, so the time is Θ(n); the average case is about n/2, also O(n).

**Answer: O(n)**

### Why the other options are wrong
- O(1): only best case (first element).
- O(log n): binary search on sorted data.
- O(n²): nested loops.

### Faster method
One loop over the data = O(n).

### Common traps
- Quoting the best case instead of the worst case.

questions.title: Complexity of R(n) = R(n-1) + 1/n
questions.statement: Consider the recurrence relation R(a) = R(a-1) + 1/a. Find the time complexity of R(n).
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0229.jpg
questions.explanation: Unrolling gives R(n) = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n = H_n, the harmonic number, which is Θ(log n).
questions.solution:
### Solution
Expand: R(n) = R(n-1) + 1/n = R(n-2) + 1/(n-1) + 1/n = ... = R(0) + sum_{k=1..n} 1/k = H_n ≈ ln n + 0.577. The harmonic series grows like ln n, so R(n) = Θ(log n).

**Answer: O(log n)**

### Why the other options are wrong
- O(n): the terms 1/k are not constants; summing n of them gives log n, not n.
- O(n log n) / O(log log n): do not match the harmonic sum.

### Faster method
Recognise the harmonic series.

### Common traps
- Treating each step as cost 1 (that would be O(n)).

questions.title: Does JavaScript pass parameters by value or reference?
questions.statement: Does JavaScript always pass parameters by value or by reference? Select the most accurate answer.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0230.jpg
questions.explanation: JavaScript always passes arguments by value. For objects the value that is copied is the reference, so mutating the object is visible to the caller, but reassigning the parameter is not.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Every argument is copied. For primitives the copy is the value; for objects the copy is the (pointer-like) reference, which is why mutations through it are visible but `param = {...}` has no effect on the caller. Technically this is call-by-sharing, still pass-by-value. JavaScript has no & operator for references.

**Answer: value**

### Why the other options are wrong
- reference: references are copied, not aliased to the caller's variable.
- depends on the parameter type: the mechanism is the same; only what is copied differs.
- &: not JavaScript syntax.

### Faster method
No pass-by-reference in JS; objects are passed by sharing.

### Common traps
- Believing object mutations prove pass-by-reference.

### Solution
JavaScript primitives are string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol and bigint. `true`, `10` and a string literal are primitives. A function is an object (it can have properties and is an instance of Function).

questions.title: Output of a closure counter called three times
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0238.jpg
questions.explanation: The IIFE creates a private counter. Post-increment returns the old value, so the three calls return 0, 1, 2; result holds the last one, 2.
questions.solution:
### Solution
The immediately invoked function runs once, creating `counter = 0` and returning the inner function (a closure). Each call returns `counter++`: the current value, then increments. Calls: 0, then 1, then 2. After the third call `result` = 2.

**Answer: 2**

### Why the other options are wrong
- Error: no error occurs.
- 0: only the first call.
- 3: that would be the counter after the call (++counter or the next value).

### Faster method
Post-increment returns the old value: three calls → 0, 1, 2.

### Common traps
- Confusing counter++ with ++counter.

questions.title: function.length with default and rest parameters
questions.statement:
Predict the output:

```js
function test(a, b = 1, c, ...args) { }
console.log(test.length)
```
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0240.jpg
questions.explanation: Function.length counts the parameters before the first one with a default value and excludes the rest parameter: only a counts.
questions.solution:
### Solution
`length` is the number of parameters expected by the function, defined as the count of parameters up to (not including) the first parameter with a default value or the rest parameter. Here the first parameter with a default is b, so only `a` counts: length = 1.

**Answer: 1**

### Why the other options are wrong
- 4: counts all parameters including b, c and the rest parameter.
- 3: counts a, b, c.
- 2: counts a and b.

### Faster method
Stop counting at the first default value.

### Common traps
- Counting c, which comes after a default parameter.

questions.title: hasOwnProperty on a class instance and an Object.create object
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0243.jpg
questions.explanation: ob1 has an own property name (class field), ob2 has none (own properties of the class constructor function are not its own), so the first comparison is true == false → false. printName is on the prototype, so both hasOwnProperty calls return false → false == false → true.
questions.solution:
### Solution
- `ob1 = new test()`: the class field `name` is created as an own property of the instance → `ob1.hasOwnProperty("name")` = true.
- `ob2 = Object.create(test)` creates a plain object whose prototype is the class constructor function; it has no own properties → false.
- First line: true == false → **false**.
- `printName` is a method defined on `test.prototype`, not an own property of ob1 → false; ob2 → false. false == false → **true**.

**Answer: false true**

### Why the other options are wrong
- true true / true false / false false: do not match the two comparisons computed above.

### Faster method
Own vs inherited: fields are own, methods are on the prototype, and Object.create(F) does not copy anything.

### Common traps
- Thinking methods defined in a class are own properties of each instance.

questions.title: What is virtual memory?
questions.statement: Identify the concept of virtual memory in an operating system.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0237.jpg

questions.explanation: Virtual memory lets processes use more address space than physical RAM by backing pages on secondary storage and swapping them in on demand.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Virtual memory maps each process's virtual addresses onto physical frames; pages not currently in RAM live on disk (swap/page file). Demand paging brings them back when needed, so disk acts as an extension of RAM.

**Answer: secondary storage used as an extension of RAM.**

### Why the other options are wrong
- Additional physical RAM: virtual memory does not add RAM.
- RAM for system processes only: unrelated.
- Graphics memory: unrelated.

### Faster method
Virtual memory = disk-backed address space.

### Common traps
- Thinking it increases physical RAM.

questions.title: Which memory section is shared between a process and its thread?
questions.statement: Which section of RAM is shared between a process and a thread?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0239.jpg
questions.explanation: Threads of a process share the heap (and also the code and data segments); each thread has its own stack. Among the options the heap is the section commonly named as shared.
questions.solution:
### Solution
A process's threads share its code (text), data (globals) and heap; only the stack (and registers) is private to each thread. So the stack is definitely not shared. The question asks for a single section; the heap is the dynamically allocated memory that threads typically share.

**Answer: Heap**

### Why the other options are wrong
- Stack: private to each thread.
- Data and Code: also shared by threads, so the question is loosely phrased.

### Faster method
Eliminate Stack; of the rest pick the commonly cited shared dynamic area: heap.

### Common traps
- Over-thinking: the data and code segments are shared too.
questions.notes: The question allows more than one correct reading since code and data are also shared among threads; heap is chosen as the usual single answer.

Core duties of an OS: process management (creation, scheduling, synchronisation), memory management (allocation, virtual memory), security/protection (access control, isolation), and performance (resource allocation, I/O scheduling, monitoring). All four options are standard responsibilities.

questions.title: Where are static, initialised static and local variables stored?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0242.jpg
questions.explanation: Uninitialised static data goes to the BSS segment, initialised static data to the data segment, and locals to the stack.
questions.solution:
### Solution
- `static int a;` is uninitialised static storage → BSS segment (zero-initialised at start).
- `static int b = 10;` is initialised static storage → data segment.
- `int c;` inside a function is an automatic variable → the stack frame of func.

**Answer: BSS, Data, Stack**

### Why the other options are wrong
- Stack, Heap, BSS: a is not on the stack and b is not on the heap.
- Heap, Code, BSS: statics are not on the heap and variables are not in the code segment.
- Data, Heap, Stack: a is in BSS (uninitialised), and b is not on the heap.

### Faster method
Initialised static → Data, uninitialised static → BSS, local → Stack, malloc → Heap.

### Common traps
- Putting uninitialised statics in the data segment.

questions.title: What is part of the C preprocessing stage?
questions.statement: Which of the following are used as part of the preprocessing stage in C? (pick one or more)

questions.explanation: Macros (#define), conditional compilation (#if/#ifdef) and include guards (#ifndef/#define/#endif) are preprocessor features; function calls are compiled and executed later.
questions.solution:
### Solution
The preprocessor handles directives starting with #: macro definition/expansion, #include, conditional compilation (#if, #ifdef, #else) and include guards, which are just conditional compilation around a header. Function calls are part of the program logic, translated by the compiler and executed at run time.

**Answer: Macros, Conditional Compilation, Include Guards.**

### Why the other options are wrong
- Function calls: not a preprocessing operation.

### Faster method
If it starts with # (or is built from # directives) it is preprocessing.

questions.title: What happens if a function calls itself infinitely?
questions.statement: What would happen if a function keeps calling itself infinitely? (pick one or more)
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0246.jpg
questions.explanation: Every call pushes a stack frame; eventually the call stack is exhausted (stack overflow), which the OS typically reports as a segmentation fault.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Each recursive call allocates a new frame (return address, parameters, locals) on the call stack, which has limited size. Without a base case the stack is exhausted: a stack overflow. In C/C++ on Linux the process then receives SIGSEGV, shown as a segmentation fault. Heap overflow and buffer overflow concern heap allocations and array bounds, not unbounded recursion.

**Answer: Stack Overflow and Segmentation Fault.**

### Why the other options are wrong
- Heap Overflow: the heap is not consumed by plain recursion.
- Buffer Overflow: that is writing past the end of an array.

### Faster method
Infinite recursion → call stack runs out.

### Common traps
- Selecting only one of the two (the second is the visible symptom).
questions.notes: Multiple-select question; the official answer is not shown.

questions.title: Fast memory allocation strategy
questions.statement: Which memory management technique is considered fast for modern-day operating systems?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\IBM Diversity Hiring Pool Campus\IMG-20240830-WA0247.jpg
questions.explanation: First Fit stops at the first hole that is large enough, so it needs less searching than Best Fit and Worst Fit, which scan all holes.
questions.solution:
### Solution
First Fit scans the free list and takes the first block that fits, so on average it examines far fewer holes than Best Fit or Worst Fit, which must scan all of them. It is also known to leave a decent fragmentation profile in practice.

**Answer: First Fit**

### Why the other options are wrong
- Best Fit: scans the entire free list and leaves tiny unusable holes.
- Worst Fit: scans the entire list and performs poorly in practice.
- Next Fit: starts the search where the previous one ended; typically no better than first fit in fragmentation.

### Faster method
Fast = stops at the first match.

### Common traps
- Next Fit is also quick; the commonly quoted answer is First Fit.
questions.notes: Next Fit is a defensible alternative; the usual textbook answer is First Fit.

questions.title: Inference from the bureaucratisation of the ruling process
questions.statement:
The greatest danger to democracy is the increasing bureaucratization of the ruling process. As bureaucracy takes control of virtually everything in governance, it becomes less accountable to both the ruling party and the legislature. There is a chance that democracy will become technocracy.

Which of the given statements can be inferred from the above information?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\IMG-20240805-WA0052.jpg
questions.explanation: The passage links growing bureaucratic control to lost accountability and then to democracy turning into technocracy. That makes accountability to the elected bodies a condition for democracy, the only option that follows without adding new claims.
questions.solution:
### Solution
An inference must follow from the passage using only what it says.
1. Passage chain: more bureaucratisation -> bureaucracy becomes less accountable to the ruling party and legislature -> democracy may become technocracy.
2. So loss of accountability is what drives democracy towards technocracy. Reversing this, accountability to the elected bodies is what keeps a system democratic.

**Answer: The accountability to both the ruling party and the legislature is key to democracy.**

### Why the other options are wrong
- "Democracy may turn into autocracy": the passage says technocracy, not autocracy.
- "Bureaucracy should be controlled...": a recommendation ("should"), not something stated or implied as fact.
- "Technocracy is not better than democracy": the passage never compares the two.

### Faster method
Look for the option that restates the passage link (accountability and democracy) without a new word such as "autocracy", "should" or "better".

### Common traps
- Mixing up an inference with a recommendation.
- Swapping one word (autocracy for technocracy).

questions.title: Reducing skill obsolescence in IT companies

Most IT organizations face a unique dilemma. They find that with every trend in the industry and in the market, their workers' knowledge and skills become obsolete. questions.explanation: Skills go stale every six months, so the remedy must be frequent, needed training. A fixed two-year cycle is too slow, a bigger budget does not guarantee frequency, and a survey only diagnoses gaps without fixing them.

questions.title: Point of disagreement in a debate on reality shows

Mr. A: The reality shows on television are affecting the moral fabric of our society. These shows present immoral behaviour as if it is the norm of society. People who watch these programs start believing that the immoral behaviour depicted in the programs is the norm of society.

questions.title: Assumption in the food-grain price argument
questions.statement:
One of the poll promises of the government in office was to control black marketing and hoarding of food grains. However, it seems that the government's initiative to control black marketing and hoarding failed in 2005. If the initiative had been successful, the price of food grains would not have gone up so much in 2005.

Which of the given is an assumption made in the above argument?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\IMG-20240805-WA0057.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\IMG-20240805-WA0058.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\IMG-20240805-WA0062.jpg
questions.explanation: The argument infers that the hoarding control failed because prices rose. This is valid only if no other cause, such as a poor harvest, pushed prices up. So the assumption is that a drop in yield was not the reason.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Conclusion: the initiative failed. Evidence: grain prices rose a lot in 2005.
2. The gap: prices could have risen for other reasons (poor harvest, imports). The argument must assume those alternatives did not cause the rise.
3. Option 2 rules out the main alternative cause (lower yield). Negation test: if yield did drop, the price rise may not show the initiative failed, and the argument breaks.
4. Option 1 contradicts the argument; options 3 and 4 concern other markets and commodities.

**Answer: A drop in the agricultural yield was not the reason for the rise in the price of food grains.**

### Why the other options are wrong
- Option 1 supplies an alternative cause, which weakens the argument.
- Option 3 is about international prices, a weaker link than domestic supply.
- Option 4 concerns other food items.

### Faster method
In cause-effect arguments the hidden assumption is usually "no other cause".

### Common traps
- Option 3 also looks like a "no other cause" statement, but option 2 targets the direct domestic supply cause.
questions.answer: A drop in the agricultural yield was not the reason for the rise in the price of food grains.
options: The supply of food grains dropped substantially in 2005.
A drop in the agricultural yield was not the reason for the rise in the price of food grains.
The price of food grains in the international market remained more or less stable.
Prices of vegetables and meat products were stable.

questions.title: What cannot be inferred about mushrooming educational institutions
questions.statement:
Mushrooming of educational institutions has led to a downfall in the levels of quality. However, it has provided an avenue for many students to get a formal education.

Which of the following CANNOT be inferred from the information given?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\IMG-20240805-WA0061.jpg
questions.explanation: The passage links the growth in institutions to lower quality and to wider access. It says nothing about what would happen with fewer institutions, so that option cannot be inferred.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. "Not all institutions provide quality education": quality has fallen, so some institutions are poor. Inferable.
2. "Educational institutions provide formal education": directly stated.
3. "Many students enrol irrespective of quality": the institutions gave an avenue to many students despite lower quality. Inferable.
4. "Fewer institutions will maintain quality": a counterfactual about a different situation. The passage does not say that reducing institutions restores quality.

**Answer: The lesser number of educational institutions will help in maintaining the quality of education.**

### Why the other options are wrong
The other three follow directly from the two sentences.

### Faster method
In a CANNOT-be-inferred question, the answer is usually the option proposing a remedy or prediction not in the text.

### Common traps
- Treating a plausible remedy as an inference.

questions.title: Conclusion best supported about ultraviolet exposure
questions.statement:
Prolonged exposure to ultraviolet rays increases the chances of developing skin cancer. Television screens, computer monitors, and water purifiers also emit ultraviolet rays.

### Solution
1. Premise A: prolonged UV exposure increases the chance of skin cancer.
2. Premise B: TVs, monitors and water purifiers emit UV.
3. Combine: those devices can (with prolonged exposure) raise the chance of skin cancer, i.e. they can cause it.

- "Must be exposed": reverses the direction (cancer need not come from these devices).

Prefer the modest "can/may" conclusion over absolute words such as primary or must.

### Common traps
- Over-strong conclusions.

questions.title: Strengthening a statement about writer's block
questions.statement:
To overcome 'writer's block', a writer needs to unwind and restart the entire thinking process so that the points that are stuck are released.

A strengthener supports the claim that unwinding fixes writer's block.

2. Option 2 gives the mechanism: unwinding produces fresh thoughts, which would release stuck points.
3. Option 3 is about need, not about the method.
4. Option 4 extends the process to cases without a block, which is irrelevant to the claim.

**Answer: Unwinding leads to fresh thoughts.**

### Why the other options are wrong
Options 1, 3 and 4 do not connect unwinding to relieving the block.

### Faster method
Choose the option that supplies the mechanism behind the stated remedy.

### Common traps
- Picking a statement that is merely related to writing.

questions.title: Assumption in the argument about mobile phones
questions.statement:
The current era is the era of communication and we are getting more and more dependent on mobile phones. However, there is an inherent problem in the use of mobile phones and hence they should be discontinued. According to a renowned psychiatrist, "Mobile phones will be a major cause of ailments in the times to come for a majority of the population."

If the above statements are true, then which of the following is an assumption made while making these statements?

questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Claim: phones have a problem (ailments), therefore discontinue them.
2. Discontinuing something useful is justified only if the cost exceeds the benefit. The passage even admits that people increasingly depend on phones.
3. So the necessary assumption is that disadvantages outweigh benefits (option 4).
4. Options 1 and 2 are unrelated statistics; option 3 names one specific ailment, but the conclusion needs the overall cost-benefit comparison.

**Answer: The disadvantages of using mobile phones outweigh their benefits.**

### Why the other options are wrong
Options 1 to 3 give side facts and are not needed for "therefore discontinue".

### Faster method
When an argument jumps from "is harmful" to "should be stopped", the missing premise is "harm outweighs benefit".

### Common traps
- Picking an option that restates an effect of phone usage.

questions.title: Sentence ordering: Sundays and tea tasting
questions.statement:

(B) Sundays are meant for leisure, where one sets aside their worries,
(C) Like any tea connoisseur, he believes that the true taste of tea can only be discovered with time.
(D) One of the things that Paul loves to do during the weekend is discover the many different varieties of teas and lay out a tasting table.

questions.solution:
### Solution
1. B is a general statement and a sentence start ("Sundays are meant for leisure, where one sets aside their worries,").
2. A starts with a lowercase gerund and continues B's sentence: "...finishing the chores left over... and spending time with family and friends". So B then A is a fixed pair.
3. D introduces the specific person (Paul) and a weekend activity.

### Why the other options are wrong
ACBD and ABCD start with A, a fragment that cannot begin a paragraph; CADB starts with "he" before Paul is introduced.

### Faster method
Find the sentence fragments that must pair (B then A), find the introduction (general before specific, name before pronoun) and test the options.

### Common traps
- Starting with a sentence that begins with a pronoun.

questions.title: Identify the error: litmus test of the depth
questions.statement:
Identify the error in the following sentence:

Being a kind, gentle soul is like a litmus test of the depth to the personality.

questions.explanation: The phrase "depth of the personality" needs "of", not "to". The other segments (Being a, soul is, test of the) are fine.

### Solution
Break the sentence into the four segments offered.
1. "Being a kind, gentle soul" is a proper gerund phrase used as subject.
2. "soul is like a litmus test" agrees in number.
3. "test of the depth" is a correct collocation (a test of something).

The other three segments are grammatically sound.

Check prepositions first; they are the most common injected error.

- Flagging "soul is" for agreement; the subject is "Being a kind, gentle soul", which is singular.

questions.title: Sentence correction: first went theirs

questions.title: Sentence correction: misplaced modifier about toys and books

### Solution

Put a "which" clause immediately after the noun it describes.

- Choosing "No error" because the sentence is understandable.

The other options keep a wrong tense, a malformed verb or the non-parallel "directing".

Fix tense first, then parallelism.

questions.title: Profit percentage when buying 20 for $15 and selling 16 for $15
questions.statement: A trader bought some items at a rate of 20 items for $15 and later sold them at a rate of 16 items for $15. Find the profit percentage for the trader.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\WhatsApp Image 2024-08-02 at 20.48.59_85613b4a.jpg
oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: Cost per item is 15/20 = $0.75 and selling price per item is 15/16 = $0.9375. Profit = 0.1875, so profit percent = 0.1875/0.75 = 25%.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Cost per item = 15/20 = 0.75. Selling price per item = 15/16 = 0.9375.
Profit = 0.9375 - 0.75 = 0.1875.
Profit % = 0.1875 / 0.75 x 100 = 25%.

**Answer: 25%**

### Why the other options are wrong

### Faster method
Pick 80 items: cost = 4 x 15 = $60; sold at 5 x 15 = $75. Profit = 15/60 = 25%.

### Common traps
- Using selling price as the base (gives 20%).

questions.title: People owning all three breeds (three-set Venn)
questions.statement: In a community of 52 members, each person has at least one pet among Dobermans, Spitzes, or Terriers. Among the members, 24 own Dobermans, 24 own Spitzes, and 35 own Terriers. No person owns more than one pet of the same breed. Additionally, there are 13 individuals who own pets of exactly two different breeds. How many people own pets of all three breeds?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\WhatsApp Image 2024-08-02 at 20.49.54_820dfdb7.jpg
oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: Let a own exactly one breed, 13 own exactly two and t own all three. People: a + 13 + t = 52. Pets: a + 26 + 3t = 83. Subtracting gives 13 + 2t = 31, so t = 9.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Let a = exactly one breed, b = exactly two (13), t = all three.
1. Members: a + b + t = 52.
2. Pet count (one pet per breed owned): a + 2b + 3t = 24 + 24 + 35 = 83.
3. Subtract: b + 2t = 31, so 13 + 2t = 31, giving t = 9. (Then a = 52 - 13 - 9 = 30; check 30 + 26 + 27 = 83.)

**Answer: 9**

### Why the other options are wrong
5, 13 and 18 fail the pet-count equation a + 2b + 3t = 83.

### Faster method
Total pets minus total people = b + 2t = 83 - 52 = 31.

### Common traps
- Using the "exactly two" count as the total of pairwise overlaps (it excludes the triple overlap).

questions.title: Colour ratio in the lower half of a painting
questions.statement: The ratio of the quantities of black, white, and blue colours used in a round canvas painting is 4 : 3 : 2 respectively. If, in the upper half of the painting, black, white, and blue colours are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 1 respectively, then what is the ratio of black, white, and blue in the lower half of the painting? (Assume equal paint in both halves.)
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\WhatsApp Image 2024-08-02 at 20.50.40_e801c22f.jpg
questions.explanation: The total ratio sum is 9, so each half has 4.5 parts. Upper half: 4.5 x (2, 3, 1)/6 = (1.5, 2.25, 0.75). Lower half = (4 - 1.5, 3 - 2.25, 2 - 0.75) = (2.5, 0.75, 1.25), which scales to 10 : 3 : 5.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Total quantity = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9 parts; assume each half uses 4.5 parts.
2. Upper half ratio 2:3:1 has sum 6, so the scale factor is 4.5/6 = 0.75: black 1.5, white 2.25, blue 0.75.
3. Lower half = total minus upper: black 2.5, white 0.75, blue 1.25.
4. Multiply by 4: 10 : 3 : 5.

**Answer: 10 : 3 : 5**

### Why the other options are wrong
Check each other option against "upper + lower = 4:3:2 with equal halves"; none works.

### Faster method
Use total = 18 parts (8, 6, 4), so 9 per half. Upper half 2:3:1 scaled to 9 is 3, 4.5, 1.5, so lower = 5, 1.5, 2.5 = 10 : 3 : 5.

### Common traps
- Forgetting each half holds equal paint.
questions.notes: The ratio 4:3:2 was read from the photo; equal quantities in both halves is the assumption that makes one option fit.

questions.title: Percent by which P's marks exceed R's
questions.statement: Three students, P, Q, and R appeared at an examination. P's marks are 50% of the sum of the marks of P, Q and R. R's marks are 60% less than the combined marks of Q and P. Find by what percent P's marks are more than R's marks.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\WhatsApp Image 2024-08-02 at 20.50.58_87fcd242.jpg
oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: P = 0.5(P+Q+R) gives P = Q + R. R = 0.4(P+Q). Substituting Q = P - R: R = 0.4(2P - R), so 1.4R = 0.8P and R = 4P/7. Then (P - R)/R = (3/7)/(4/7) = 75%.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. P = 50% of (P+Q+R) means P = Q + R, so Q = P - R.
2. R is 60% less than (Q+P): R = 0.4(Q+P) = 0.4(2P - R) => R = 0.8P - 0.4R => 1.4R = 0.8P => R = 4P/7.
3. Q = 3P/7 (check: Q + R = P).
4. P exceeds R by (P - R)/R = (3P/7)/(4P/7) = 3/4 = 75%.

**Answer: 75%**

### Why the other options are wrong
50% and 25% come from using P as the base; "cannot be determined" fails because the ratio is fixed.

### Faster method
Let P = 7, then Q = 3, R = 4. (7 - 4)/4 = 75%.

### Common traps
- Computing the difference as a percent of P instead of R.

questions.title: Three numbers in doubling progression with average of last two
questions.statement: Three numbers are given, the first number is half the second, and the second number is half the third. If the average of the second and third numbers is 93, determine the value of the first number.

questions.solution:
### Solution
Let the first number be x; the others are 2x and 4x. (2x + 4x)/2 = 3x = 93, so x = 31.

**Answer: 31**

### Why the other options are wrong
Other options do not give 3x = 93.

### Faster method
The average of the last two is 3 times the first number, so first = 93/3.

- Taking the first number as half of 93.

### Solution
3 couples become 3 blocks arranged in 3! = 6 ways. Inside each block the two partners can be ordered in 2 ways, giving 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.
Total = 6 x 8 = 48.

**Answer: 48**

### Why the other options are wrong
12 and 24 ignore the internal swaps; 120 = 5! is arbitrary.

n! x 2^n with n = 3.

- Forgetting the internal swap factor 2^3.

questions.title: Selling price per chocolate for 25 percent profit after a loss
questions.statement: A shopkeeper sells 5 chocolates for $4 and incurs a loss of $2 in the transaction. At what price should he sell each chocolate to make a profit of 25%?

### Solution
The sale price of 5 chocolates is $4 with a $2 loss, so their cost price is $6, i.e. $1.2 each.
For 25% profit: 1.2 x 1.25 = $1.5.

**Answer: $1.5**

### Why the other options are wrong
$1.2 is the cost price; $2 and $2.5 are too high.

### Faster method
CP = SP + loss; then multiply by 1.25.

### Common traps
- Using $4/5 = $0.8 as the cost price.

questions.title: Commission as a percent of basic pay
questions.statement: A man's salary comprises basic pay (fixed) and commission. In a particular month, he got 20% less commission than in the previous month, and as a result, his total salary was reduced by 5%. The commission he received last month was what percent of the basic pay?
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: Let basic = B and last month commission = C. The 20% drop in commission (0.2C) equals 5% of the previous total: 0.2C = 0.05(B + C), so 0.15C = 0.05B and C = B/3.
questions.solution:
### Solution
The fall in salary equals the fall in commission: 0.2C = 0.05(B + C).
0.2C - 0.05C = 0.05B -> 0.15C = 0.05B -> C = B/3 = 33.33% of B.

**Answer: 33.33%**

### Why the other options are wrong
Other values do not satisfy 0.2C = 0.05(B + C).

### Faster method
20% of C is 5% of (B + C), so C : (B + C) = 1 : 4, hence C : B = 1 : 3.

### Common traps
- Using this month's total as the base for the 5% reduction.

questions.title: Number to add to 5, 17, 41, 89 to make them proportional
questions.statement: What number should be added to each of the numbers 5, 17, 41, and 89 so that they are in proportion?
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.solution:
### Solution
Condition: (5+x)/(17+x) = (41+x)/(89+x).
Cross multiply: 445 + 94x + x^2 = 697 + 58x + x^2 -> 36x = 252 -> x = 7.
Check: 12, 24, 48, 96 are in ratio 1:2:4:8, so 12:24 = 48:96.

**Answer: 7**

### Why the other options are wrong
x = 3 gives 8:20 vs 44:92; x = 5 gives 10:22 vs 46:94; x = 8 gives 13:25 vs 49:97; none are equal.

### Faster method
Plug the options: 7 gives 12, 24, 48, 96.

### Common traps
- Forgetting that the x^2 terms cancel.

questions.title: Ratio of salaries in March after percentage changes
questions.statement: In a particular year, the salaries of employees P and Q in January were in the ratio of 3 : 2, respectively. P's salary ratio for January and February was 4 : 5, while Q's salary ratio for January and February was 2 : 3. In March, P's salary decreased by 20% and Q's salary decreased by 25% from their respective previous month's salary. What is the ratio of the salaries of P and Q in March, respectively?
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: Take January salaries P = 12, Q = 8. February: P = 15, Q = 12. March: P = 12, Q = 9. Ratio 12 : 9 = 4 : 3.
questions.solution:
### Solution
January: P = 12, Q = 8 (3 : 2 scaled by 4).
February: P = 12 x 5/4 = 15, Q = 8 x 3/2 = 12.
March: P = 15 x 0.8 = 12, Q = 12 x 0.75 = 9.
Ratio = 12 : 9 = 4 : 3.

**Answer: 4 : 3**

### Why the other options are wrong
The other ratios come from applying the decreases to the wrong month.

### Faster method
Use P = 12, Q = 8 so every step stays an integer.

### Common traps
- Applying the percentage decreases to January salaries.

questions.title: Percentage of students in the dance competition
questions.statement: In a college fest, 40% of the students participated in the painting competition, and 20% of those who participated in the painting competition also participated in the dance competition. If 40% of the students participated in neither the dance nor the painting competition, what is the percentage of students who participated in the dance competition?
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: Painting 40%, both = 20% of 40 = 8%, neither = 40% so union = 60%. Dance = union - painting + both = 60 - 40 + 8 = 28%.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Union = 100 - 40 = 60%.
Both = 0.2 x 40 = 8%.
Union = Painting + Dance - Both -> 60 = 40 + D - 8 -> D = 28%.

**Answer: 28%**

### Why the other options are wrong
20%, 32% and 40% do not satisfy the union equation.

### Faster method
Dance = 60 - 40 + 8.

### Common traps
- Forgetting to add back the overlap.

questions.title: Arrangements of JUDGE with all consonants not together
questions.statement: In how many ways can the letters of the word JUDGE be arranged so that all consonants are not together?
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: The word has 5 distinct letters (120 arrangements). Consonants J, D, G; vowels U, E. Arrangements with all three consonants together = 3! x 3! = 36. So 120 - 36 = 84.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Total arrangements = 5! = 120.
Consonants J, D, G together: treat them as one block, so 3 units (block, U, E) are arranged in 3! = 6 ways; inside the block 3! = 6 ways. 6 x 6 = 36.
Required = 120 - 36 = 84.

**Answer: 84**

### Why the other options are wrong
72 would be 120 - 48; 65 and 114 do not come from any valid count.

### Faster method
Complement: total minus "together".

### Common traps
- Reading "not together" as "no two consonants adjacent" (that would give 12).

questions.title: Starting direction from turns
questions.statement: Mr. X travelled a certain distance straight ahead from station A. He then turned left and travelled some more distance to reach station B. Finally, he turned to his right from station B and travelled some more distance. If he was finally facing South, in which direction did he start the journey?
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: A left turn and then a right turn cancel each other, so the final facing direction equals the starting direction. He finally faces South, so he started facing South.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Starting direction = d. After turning left he faces d rotated 90 degrees anticlockwise; turning right then rotates 90 degrees clockwise, back to d. Final direction = d = South.

**Answer: South**

### Why the other options are wrong
Any other start would end in a different final direction.

### Faster method
Left followed by right means no net turn.

### Common traps
- Thinking the two turns point you in a new direction.

questions.title: Position of R between two interchanged ranks
questions.statement: In a class test ranking, each student secured a unique position. 'P' holds the 27th position from the top, while 'Q' holds the 24th position from the bottom. If they interchange their positions, 'P' will then occupy the 13th position from the top. If 'R' is positioned exactly between 'P' and 'Q', what will be R's position from the top?
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: After the interchange P takes Q's old place, so Q was 13th from the top. P was 27th. R is exactly midway: (13 + 27)/2 = 20th from the top.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Q originally = 13th from the top (that is the seat P gets). P originally = 27th. The middle of 13 and 27 is (13 + 27)/2 = 20, with 6 students between 13 and 20 and 6 between 20 and 27. (Total students = 13 + 23 = 36.)

**Answer: 20th**

### Why the other options are wrong
15th, 23rd and 19th are not midway between 13 and 27.

### Faster method
Midpoint formula.

### Common traps
- Using the interchanged positions for R.

questions.title: Weights of bags: truth of the third statement
questions.statement:
There are four bags, A, B, C, and D, with different weights loaded onto a wagon. It is known that:
I. Bag B is heavier than bag D but not the heaviest.
II. Bag C is heavier than bag D but lighter than bag A.
III. Only one bag is heavier than bag B.

If the first two statements are true, what can be said about the third statement?
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: From I and II: A > C > D and B > D, B not heaviest. B could be between A and C (A > B > C > D, only A heavier: III true) or between C and D (A > C > B > D, two bags heavier: III false). So it is uncertain.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Known: A > C > D, B > D, and B is not the heaviest.
Case 1: A > B > C > D. Only A is heavier than B: III true.
Case 2: A > C > B > D. A and C are heavier than B: III false.
Both cases fit statements I and II, so the third statement is uncertain.

**Answer: Uncertain**

### Why the other options are wrong
"True" and "False" each fail in one valid arrangement.

### Faster method
Enumerate where the unconstrained bag can sit.

### Common traps
- Assuming B is directly below A.

questions.title: Six girls seated in a row: who sits at the ends
questions.statement:
Six girls Jasmine, Kara, Linda, Megan, Nora, and Oliver are sitting in a row facing North, but not necessarily in the same order.
- Kara is sitting third to the right of Linda.
- The number of people to the left of Kara is the same as the number of people to the right of Linda.
- Megan and Nora are sitting adjacent to each other.

Who among the given pairs is sitting at the end of the row?
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\zs associates\ZS  .pdf
questions.explanation: Number seats 1 to 6 from left to right. If Linda is at L, Kara is at L + 3, and K - 1 = 6 - L gives L = 2, K = 5. Megan and Nora must be adjacent in the remaining seats {1, 3, 4, 6}, so they take 3 and 4. Jasmine and Oliver take the ends 1 and 6.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Facing North, right means a higher seat number. Kara = Linda + 3.
2. People to Kara's left = K - 1; people to Linda's right = 6 - L. Equal: L + 2 = 6 - L -> L = 2, K = 5.
3. Free seats: 1, 3, 4, 6. Megan and Nora need adjacent seats: only 3 and 4.
4. Jasmine and Oliver fill 1 and 6, the two ends.

**Answer: Oliver and Jasmine**

### Why the other options are wrong
Linda (seat 2) and Kara (seat 5) are not at the ends.

### Faster method
The equation from the two counts gives Linda and Kara; adjacency pushes the others to the ends.

### Common traps
- Reading "right" as the viewer's right instead of the girls' right.

questions.title: Who owns the Audi among three friends

Three friends, Jassi, Kane, and Roman, have three different cars, namely Audi, Ferrari, and Mercedes, of three different colours Red, White, and Yellow, not necessarily in the same order.

questions.title: Estimate the daily footfall of the Dubai Mall
questions.statement:
You are shown a set of statements. Use the data in these statements to find the answer to the question. Not all the data may be relevant. Round decimal answers to the next whole number.

Relevant statements: 8) In 2008 the total footfall was 32 million in a year, and since then the number of visitors increased by 20%, then 24%, then 28%, then 23% and 25% in the following years. 14) The days of 2013 are used for calculation (365 days). 15) Footfalls include visitors and workers. 16) The mall is open 24 hours a day. (Other statements cover shops, workers, parking, revenue and hours.)

How many people footfall into Dubai Mall in a day?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\WhatsApp Image 2024-08-02 at 20.39.23_17e0af9b.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\WhatsApp Image 2024-08-02 at 20.39.36_5300d67b.jpg
questions.explanation: Footfall in 2013 = 32 million x 1.20 x 1.24 x 1.28 x 1.23 x 1.25 = 93,708,288. Dividing by 365 days gives 256,735.7, which rounds up to 256,736 per day. The worker, parking and revenue statements are distractors because footfall already includes workers.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. 2009: 32 x 1.20 = 38.4 million.
2. 2010: 38.4 x 1.24 = 47.616 million.
3. 2011: 47.616 x 1.28 = 60.948 million.
4. 2012: 60.948 x 1.23 = 74.966 million.
5. 2013: 74.966 x 1.25 = 93.708 million (93,708,288).
6. Per day: 93,708,288 / 365 = 256,735.7, rounded up to the next whole number = 256,736.

**Answer: 256,736 people per day**

### Faster method
Multiply the growth factors first: 1.2 x 1.24 x 1.28 x 1.23 x 1.25 = 2.928384, then 32M x 2.928384 / 365.

### Common traps
- Starting the growth in 2008 instead of 2009 (the first increase gives 2009).
- Adding workers on top of the footfall, although statement 15 says they are included.
- Using 366 or 360 days.
questions.notes: Interpretation: statement 15 says footfalls include visitors and workers, so no extra worker count is added. If the intended answer adds workers separately the number would differ.

questions.title: Estimate the number of movie halls in Delhi
questions.statement:
Use the statements to find the number of movie halls in Delhi (round up to the next whole number).

1) Delhi population is 22 million. 2) Total average monthly revenue is Rs 1.2 billion. 3) Average ticket price is Rs 200. 4) 10 movies run on any day. 5) About 30% of the population is below 14 years. 6) About 5% is above 60 years. 7) 5% of children below 14 and 5% of people above 60 go for an average of one movie per month. 8) 20% of the population in the 14-60 age group go for an average of 2 movies per month. 9) 80% of the halls are multiplexes (4 screens) and 20% are single-screen halls. 10) Average optimum capacity per screen is 300. 11) Monday to Friday average occupancy is 40% and on Saturday-Sunday 70%. 12) There are on average 4 shows per screen per day.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\WhatsApp Image 2024-08-05 at 20.30.37_f00850f9.jpg
questions.explanation: Monthly tickets: children 22M x 0.30 x 0.05 = 0.33M, seniors 22M x 0.05 x 0.05 = 0.055M, adults (65%) 14.3M x 0.20 x 2 = 5.72M, total 6.105M. Average screens per hall = 0.8 x 4 + 0.2 x 1 = 3.4. Weekly average occupancy = (5 x 0.4 + 2 x 0.7)/7 = 0.4857. Tickets per screen per month = 4 x 300 x 0.4857 x 30 = 17,486. Per hall = 3.4 x 17,486 = 59,451. Halls = 6.105M / 59,451 = 102.7, so 103.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Match demand (tickets per month) with the supply per hall.

**Demand**
1. Children below 14: 22M x 30% = 6.6M; 5% watch 1 film -> 0.33M.
2. Above 60: 22M x 5% = 1.1M; 5% watch 1 film -> 0.055M.
3. Ages 14-60: 65% = 14.3M; 20% watch 2 films -> 14.3M x 0.2 x 2 = 5.72M.
4. Total tickets per month = 6.105M.

**Supply per hall**
5. Average screens per hall = 0.8 x 4 + 0.2 x 1 = 3.4.
6. Average occupancy = (5 x 40% + 2 x 70%)/7 = 48.57%.
7. Tickets per screen per month = 4 shows x 300 seats x 0.4857 x 30 days = 17,486.
8. Per hall = 3.4 x 17,486 = 59,451.

**Answer:** 6,105,000 / 59,451 = 102.7, rounded up to **103 halls**.

### Faster method
Compute total demand once, then one blended hall capacity, and divide.

### Common traps
- Using 4 screens for every hall.
- Using 40% occupancy for all days.
- Treating "Rs 1.2 billion per hall" literally; the revenue is for Delhi as a whole (6.105M x Rs 200 = Rs 1.22 billion, consistent with the demand).
questions.notes: Estimation question; another route (revenue Rs 1.2 billion / Rs 200 = 6 million tickets) gives about 101 halls. The 103 figure follows the demographic statements 5 to 8. A month is taken as 30 days.

questions.title: Estimate daytime passengers through T3 of IGI Airport
questions.statement:
Use the statements to estimate the number of people who fly in and out of T3 of Indira Gandhi International Airport, New Delhi during day time (7 am to 8 pm). Round to the next whole number.

Relevant statements: peak traffic is 7-10 am and 3-8 pm; an average plane is at 100% capacity only at peak, and at 50% off-peak and 75% mid-peak; a plane lands or takes off every 5 minutes at peak, every 10 minutes at mid-peak and every 15 minutes off-peak; an aircraft carries 200 passengers at full capacity; 10 am to 3 pm is mid-peak; 8 pm to 11 pm is mild traffic. (The remaining statements on area, runway, counters and ranking are distractors.)
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\WhatsApp Image 2024-08-05 at 20.30.37_c0a2b7f6.jpg
questions.explanation: Peak hours 7-10 am and 3-8 pm total 8 hours: 12 flights per hour x 8 = 96 flights at 200 passengers = 19,200. Mid-peak 10 am-3 pm is 5 hours: 6 flights per hour x 5 = 30 flights at 150 passengers = 4,500. Total = 23,700.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Daytime 7 am to 8 pm = 13 hours = peak 8 h (7-10 and 3-8) + mid-peak 5 h (10-3). Off-peak does not occur in this window.
1. Peak: a flight every 5 min = 12 per hour. 12 x 8 = 96 flights, each full: 96 x 200 = 19,200.
2. Mid-peak: a flight every 10 min = 6 per hour. 6 x 5 = 30 flights at 75%: 30 x 150 = 4,500.
3. Total = 19,200 + 4,500 = 23,700.

**Answer: 23,700 people**

### Faster method
Flights x capacity: (96 x 200) + (30 x 150).

### Common traps
- Counting off-peak hours (8 pm to 11 pm is outside 7 am to 8 pm).
- Doubling for "in and out"; every landing or take-off is a separate flight event already counted by the frequency.

questions.title: Hungry Kya!: profit of the most profitable circle
questions.statement:
Hungry Kya! plans to launch a cloud kitchen service in the eastern metropolitan Pianchi. Pianchi is divided into 6 circles, each with roughly equal population. Outlets are expected to receive 180K orders per month across Pianchi at an Average Order Value (AOV) of INR 500 (assume equal distribution of orders and revenue across circles). Field research shows Hungry Kya! will have to set up 5 kitchens in Circle 1 to support the demand (assume each kitchen covers an equal area irrespective of circle/density). Average monthly cost per kitchen: INR 1,000,000.

Population density (per sq. mile): Circle 1: 300, Circle 2: 200, Circle 3: 150, Circle 4: 75, Circle 5: 250, Circle 6: 100.

Question 1.2: What is the estimated maximum profit that Hungry Kya! can achieve from its most profitable region, considering they launch in select regions?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\zs case study\WhatsApp Image 2024-09-05 at 19.09.06.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\zs case study\WhatsApp Image 2024-09-05 at 19.09.11.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\zs case study\WhatsApp Image 2024-09-05 at 19.09.13.jpeg
questions.explanation: Revenue per circle = 180,000 x 500 / 6 = INR 15,000,000 per month. With equal population, area is proportional to 1/density, and one kitchen covers the area of Circle 1 divided by 5, so kitchens needed = 1500/density: C1 5, C2 7.5, C3 10, C4 20, C5 6, C6 15. Profit = 15M - kitchens x 1M: C1 10M, C2 7.5M, C3 5M, C4 -5M, C5 9M, C6 0. The most profitable circle is Circle 1 with INR 10 million.
questions.solution:
### Solution
**Step 1: revenue per circle.** Total orders 180,000 x INR 500 = INR 90,000,000 per month; equal across 6 circles = INR 15,000,000 each.

**Step 2: kitchens needed per circle.** Populations are equal, so area is proportional to 1/density. A kitchen covers a fixed area, so kitchens needed is proportional to 1/density. Circle 1 needs 5 kitchens at density 300, so kitchens = 5 x 300 / density = 1500/density.

| Circle | Density | Kitchens | Cost (INR M) | Profit (INR M) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 300 | 5 | 5 | 10 |
| 2 | 200 | 7.5 | 7.5 | 7.5 |
| 3 | 150 | 10 | 10 | 5 |
| 4 | 75 | 20 | 20 | -5 |
| 5 | 250 | 6 | 6 | 9 |
| 6 | 100 | 15 | 15 | 0 |

**Step 3.** Launching only in profitable circles (1, 2, 3, 5) avoids the loss in Circle 4 and the break-even in Circle 6. The best single circle is Circle 1 with **INR 10,000,000 per month**.

### Faster method
Kitchens = 1500/density; profit = 15 - kitchens (in INR million).

### Common traps
- Forgetting that denser circles need fewer kitchens (the area per kitchen is fixed).
- Dividing the revenue by circle area; revenue is equal per circle.

questions.title: Hungry Kya!: best expected return from splitting the marketing budget
questions.statement:
In advance of launching the new service, Hungry Kya! wants to streamline its annual marketing budget (INR 100 lakhs) to achieve more impact and sales growth from the same amount of money spent. A line chart shows expected returns (in MN) for Social Media, Online, TV, Print and Telemarketing against the percentage of the annual advertising budget spent on each channel.

Question 3: What is the maximum expected return from the best allocation of the budget across channels?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\zs case study\WhatsApp Image 2024-09-05 at 19.09.14.jpeg
questions.explanation: Read each channel curve at 10% steps and choose the split of 100% that maximises the sum. Approximate reading: Social Media 30% -> 70, Online 10% -> 20, TV 50% -> 60, Print 10% -> 10, Telemarketing 0%. Total about 160 MN = INR 16 crore.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Approach: a knapsack-style allocation. Split 100% of the budget in 10% steps among channels so that the sum of expected returns is maximal.
1. Read the chart (approximate, MN): Social Media 10% -> 5, 20% -> 50, 30% -> 70, 40%+ -> 80; Online 10% -> 20, 70% -> 75; TV 10% -> 15, 50% -> 60; Print 10% -> 10, 60% -> 65, 70% -> 70; Telemarketing low everywhere.
2. Dynamic programming over channels gives the best total with Social 30%, Online 10%, TV 50%, Print 10%: 70 + 20 + 60 + 10 = 160 MN.
3. 160 MN = INR 16,00,00,000.

**Answer: INR 16,00,00,000** (confidence low because the curve values are read by eye).

### Why the other options are wrong
INR 16.5 crore would need chart readings about 5 MN higher; 15.5 and 15 crore are below the best split found.

### Faster method
Social Media saturates at about 40%, so put only as much there as the steep part needs, then give the rest to the next best curves.

### Common traps
- Putting everything on the single best channel.
- Ignoring diminishing or even falling returns (TV and Online drop after their peak).

questions.title: Hungry Kya!: which service factors need focus compared with the competitor
questions.statement:
A survey asked customers to rate features of Hungry Kya! (n = 300) and a competitor (n = 350) on a scale of 1 to 5 (5 is best). For Hungry Kya!: surge pricing 80% gave 5; time to delivery 30% gave 5; cuisine variety 80% gave 5; missing orders 20% gave 5; discounts 90% gave 1; ease of ordering 95% gave 5; restaurant ratings 90% gave 5. For the competitor: surge pricing 79% gave 5; time to delivery 50% gave 5; cuisine variety 78% gave 5; missing orders 50% gave 5; discounts 90% gave 5; ease of ordering 95% gave 5; restaurant ratings 50% gave 5.

Question 3: Which factors does Hungry Kya! need to focus on?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\zs case study\WhatsApp Image 2024-09-05 at 19.09.25.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\zs case study\WhatsApp Image 2024-09-05 at 19.09.27.jpeg
questions.explanation: Compare the share of top ratings: Hungry Kya! lags the competitor on discounts (90% rate it 1 against 90% rating it 5), on time to delivery (30% against 50% top rating) and on missing orders (20% against 50%). Surge pricing, cuisine variety and ease of ordering are on par, and restaurant ratings are better.
questions.solution:
### Approach
Compare each feature across the two bar charts and find where Hungry Kya! is clearly worse.

### Comparison (share giving the top rating of 5 unless stated)
| Feature | Hungry Kya! | Competitor | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Surge pricing | 80% | 79% | on par |
| Time to delivery | 30% | 50% | behind |
| Cuisine variety | 80% | 78% | on par |
| Missing orders | 20% | 50% | behind |
| Discounts | 90% rate it 1 (poor) | 90% rate it 5 | far behind |
| Ease of ordering | 95% | 95% | on par |
| Restaurant ratings | 90% | 50% | ahead |

### Recommendation
Focus on **discounts** (largest gap), **time to delivery** and **missing orders** (operational reliability). Keep investing lightly where it already equals or beats the competitor, and use the restaurant-ratings advantage in marketing.

### Likely follow-ups
- **Which one first?** Discounts, because it is the biggest satisfaction gap and the cheapest lever to pull.
- **How would you measure improvement?** Re-run the same survey and track top-rating share and repeat-order rate for each feature.
- **Why not surge pricing?** Ratings there are already equal to the competitor.
questions.answer: Discounts, time to delivery and missing orders
questions.notes: Percentages were read from stacked bar charts in angled photos; the options of the original question were not visible, so this is recorded as an open question.

questions.title: SQL: names of trains whose description is LUXURY
questions.statement: Write an SQL query (MySQL 8.0) to display the train names whose description is LUXURY. Your output should contain one column: Train_Name. (The database schema was shown only inside the test tool, so the table and column names below are assumed.)
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\zs case study\WhatsApp Image 2024-09-05 at 19.09.21.jpeg
questions.explanation: Join the train table to the train-type table on the type code and filter on the description. The schema was not visible, so the names are assumed.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
The luxury label lives in a lookup table of train types, while train names live in the train table, so we need a join.

### Approach
1. Join `train` with `train_type` on the type code.
2. Keep the rows whose description equals LUXURY.
3. Select only the train name and alias it as `Train_Name`.

### Why it works
An inner join keeps only trains with a known type; the equality filter selects those typed as LUXURY.

### Complexity
O(n + m) with hash joins, or O(n log m) with an index on `type_code`.

### SQL solution
```sql
SELECT t.train_name AS Train_Name
FROM train t
JOIN train_type tt ON t.type_code = tt.type_code
WHERE tt.type_description = 'LUXURY';
```

### Dry run
If train_type has (LUX, LUXURY) and train has (Maharajas Express, LUX), (Local Fast, PSNG), the join gives one row for Maharajas Express which passes the filter.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Case or trailing spaces in the description: use `UPPER(TRIM(...))` if the data are messy.
- If the description is stored on the train table itself, no join is needed.
- Use the exact output column name required.
questions.answer: SELECT t.train_name AS Train_Name FROM train t JOIN train_type tt ON t.type_code = tt.type_code WHERE tt.type_description = 'LUXURY';
questions.notes: The schema was only available in the test tool. Table and column names (train, train_type, train_name, type_code, type_description) are assumptions.

questions.title: SQL: express and passenger trains with start and destination codes
questions.statement: Write a MySQL query to find the train name, type description, code of the starting station and code of the destination station (for example NDLS for New Delhi) of all express and passenger trains. The output should contain 4 columns in this order: train_name, type_description, train_from, train_to. Hint: train types are abbreviated; Express is stored as "EXP" and Passenger as "PSNG". (The schema was not visible in the photo; names below are assumed.)
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\zs associates\zs case study\WhatsApp Image 2024-09-05 at 19.09.24.jpeg
questions.explanation: Join trains with their type and keep types EXP and PSNG with IN. Output the four requested columns in order. Station codes are assumed to be stored directly on the train table.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
We need train attributes plus the textual type description, filtered to two codes.

### Approach
1. Join `train` to `train_type` on the type code.
2. Filter `type_code IN ('EXP', 'PSNG')`.
3. Select the columns in the order given: name, description, from-code, to-code.

### Why it works
The join attaches the description to each train and the `IN` filter keeps only the requested categories.

### Complexity
O(n + m) with a hash join (or an indexed join).

### SQL solution
```sql
SELECT t.train_name,
       tt.type_description,
       t.train_from,
       t.train_to
FROM train t
JOIN train_type tt ON t.type_code = tt.type_code
WHERE t.type_code IN ('EXP', 'PSNG');
```

### Dry run
Rows (Rajdhani, EXP, NDLS, BCT), (Local, PSNG, ...), (Luxury Special, LUX, ...) give two output rows: the LUX train is filtered out.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- If station codes live in a `station` table, join it twice with aliases (one for from, one for to).
- Column order matters when the checker compares output.
- Do not use `LIKE '%EXP%'`, which could also match other codes.
questions.answer: SELECT t.train_name, tt.type_description, t.train_from, t.train_to FROM train t JOIN train_type tt ON t.type_code = tt.type_code WHERE t.type_code IN ('EXP', 'PSNG');
questions.notes: Schema not visible; table and column names are assumed. If station codes are in a separate stations table, two extra joins on from/to ids are needed.

questions.title: Organisation of a passage on intellectual property rights
questions.statement:
The passage explains that globalisation has raised the importance of intellectual property rights (IPRs); that firms with significant IPRs hold considerable power, especially in technology; that economists say the social benefits (innovation and creativity) outweigh monopolistic consequences while critics say IPRs stifle innovation and let firms limit competition and raise prices; and that the digital age is pushing the boundaries of traditional IPR frameworks, prompting regulators to balance rewarding innovation against the risks of monopolies.

Which of the following best describes the author's organization of the passage?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\20240908_111150.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\20240908_111156.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0132.jpeg
questions.explanation: The passage opens with why IPRs matter, then gives the pro and con arguments, and closes with the regulators' balancing role. Only the first option follows that order.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Map each paragraph block to its function.
1. Opening: globalisation raises the significance of IPRs and why firms guard them (importance).
2. Middle: economists (benefits) versus critics (stifled innovation, high prices) -> positive and negative consequences.
3. Close: the digital age strains old frameworks and regulators must balance reward and monopoly risk -> regulators' role.
This is exactly option A.

**Answer: A**

### Why the other options are wrong
- B: the author never critiques first and then defends.
- C: there is no history or evolution section.
- D: the author does not take a neutral "equal arguments" stance; the passage also covers regulators.

### Faster method
Write a three-word skeleton of the passage (importance, pros/cons, regulation) and match it to the options.

### Common traps
- Choosing the "neutral stance" option because both sides appear; structure questions ask about order, not tone.
questions.answer: The author discusses the importance of Intellectual Property Rights, outlines its positive and negative consequences, and finally discusses the role of regulatory bodies
options: The author discusses the importance of Intellectual Property Rights, outlines its positive and negative consequences, and finally discusses the role of regulatory bodies
The author critiques Intellectual Property Rights before defending its importance in the modern economy
The author provides a brief introduction of Intellectual Property Rights, discusses its history and evolution, and wraps up with its future prospects
The author maintains a neutral stance, providing equal arguments for and against Intellectual Property Rights
questions.notes: The passage was photographed in two parts; the summary above paraphrases it.

questions.title: Logical structure of a passage on modern marketing
questions.statement:
The passage says that integrating traditional marketing with digital media has created "modern marketing": technology is used for data collection, audience targeting and analytics, giving higher return on investment. It then explains how HR roles are changing from hiring and firing to strategic decision-making, how regulators grapple with digital technology, and concludes that modern marketing is "a montage of technological changes reinforcing traditional business domains".

What is the logical structure of the passage?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0124.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0126.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0128.jpeg
questions.explanation: The first sentence introduces the concept; the rest elaborate its use, then its effects on HR and regulation, ending with a summary line. There is no opposing view or narrative.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Para opens by defining "modern marketing" (concept introduced).
2. It then elaborates technology uses, impact on HR and on regulation (elaborations and implications).
3. It closes with a one-line synthesis. Nothing is critiqued, no contrary view is given, and it is not a story.

**Answer: Introduction of a concept followed by elaborations, examples and implications**

### Why the other options are wrong
A, B and E need an opposing view or critique, which the passage lacks; D needs a sequence of events.

### Faster method
Look for words such as "however" or "critics". None appear, so eliminate options needing opposition.

### Common traps
- Reading "traditional vs digital" as two opposing concepts; the passage says they reinforce each other.
questions.answer: Introduction of a concept followed by elaborations, examples and implications
options: Presentation of a concept followed by contrary ideas
Presentation of an idea followed by critique and conclusion
Introduction of a concept followed by elaborations, examples and implications
Narration of an event from start to finish

questions.title: Completion of an argument on flexible work hours for designers
questions.statement:
A design agency is contemplating flexible work hours for its graphic designers within a time window from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.

This policy could likely undermine project completion if the designers' responsibilities involve them needing to ______.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0134.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0136.jpeg
questions.explanation: Flexible, non-overlapping hours hurt tasks that depend on real-time collaboration. Frequent input from colleagues is the only option that depends on others being present at the same time.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Flexible hours let each person choose when to work in a 12-hour window, so overlap with colleagues shrinks.
- Software use, design principles and client expectations can be handled alone at any hour.
- Tight deadlines are affected by total hours, not by the time of day.
- Frequent colleague feedback needs others to be available at the same time, so it is the responsibility that flexible timing can undermine.

**Answer: seek frequent input and feedback from their colleagues**

### Why the other options are wrong
The other four are individual tasks that do not depend on when others are working.

### Faster method
Find the option that needs other people at the same moment.

### Common traps
- Picking "tight deadlines"; flexibility does not remove hours.
questions.answer: seek frequent input and feedback from their colleagues
options: seek frequent input and feedback from their colleagues
adhere to the established design principles
ensure their designs meet client expectations

questions.title: Best plan to prepare healthcare staff for telecare
questions.statement:
Given the rapid growth of telecare in healthcare, traditional roles within the sector are transforming substantially. Within the next five years, healthcare professionals will require new skills to adapt effectively to these technologies.

Which of the following plans, if feasible, would enable a healthcare organization to prepare most effectively for this impending change?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0144.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0146.jpeg
questions.explanation: The need is new skills within five years, so the best plan is ongoing, needed training. Surveys only observe, an awareness programme informs without training, and training six years in is too late.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Requirement: staff need new skills before about five years pass.
- A: continuous, necessary training builds the skills in time and keeps up with change.
- B: surveys measure the impact but do not build skills.
- C: an educational programme informs staff about repercussions, which is awareness and not skill building, and only happens once.
- D: only select employees and after six years, past the five-year window.

**Answer: A**

### Why the other options are wrong
See steps B, C and D above.

### Faster method
Check each plan for who is trained, what is taught and when.

### Common traps
- Option C sounds proactive, but informing is not training.
questions.answer: The organization commits to providing continuous necessary training to meet the evolving demand of its employees in the rapidly changing telecare-integrated healthcare field.
options: The organization commits to providing continuous necessary training to meet the evolving demand of its employees in the rapidly changing telecare-integrated healthcare field.
The organization contemplates conducting periodic surveys to understand the impacts of telecare integration on its employees role.
Before telecare implementation, the organization intends to conduct an educational program to inform staff of the likely repercussions.
The organization proposes offering specific telecare training to select employees six years into service.

questions.title: Main point of a passage on economics, marketing and HR in business success
questions.statement:
The passage argues that a deep understanding of economic fundamentals (supply and demand, GDP, inflation, interest rates) is said to matter more than academic qualifications for entrepreneurs; marketing experts counter that understanding customer needs underpins strategy; HR researchers say success depends on the people who create, manage and sell the product; studies concluded that the three fields hold equitable significance, yet in practice undue importance is given to one field depending on the business environment.

Which among the following best articulates the main point of the passage?

Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0150.jpeg
questions.explanation: The passage presents economists, marketers and HR researchers each claiming primacy, then notes the studies find equal importance. Its main point is the debate among fields about importance, not any single field.

### Solution
The main point must cover the whole passage.
1. Options A, B and E each describe only one field, so they are too narrow.
2. Option D (changing emphasis) is only the last sentence and is a detail about practice.
3. Option C covers all three fields claiming importance and the conclusion that they are equally significant.

**Answer: The debate among different fields on their importance in running a successful business**

### Why the other options are wrong
A, B, E are too narrow; D covers only the final sentence.

### Faster method
Main-point options that name one subject are usually traps when the passage lists several.

### Common traps
- Choosing the first field mentioned (economics).

questions.title: Flaw in the data analyst's argument about the DeepThought model
questions.statement:
AI Developer: The AI model DeepThought has shown promise in predictive analytics. However, the long-term impacts on data integrity are still unknown, and for that reason, I am not advocating for its wide use currently.

Data Analyst: Your viewpoint opposes your usual actions. You implement models that you know can potentially lead to data issues, so surely concern about impacts isn't why you won't endorse DeepThought.

The data analyst's argument is flawed because it fails to consider that ______.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0152.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0154.jpeg
questions.explanation: The developer accepts models with known, weighable risks but hesitates over DeepThought whose risk is unknown. The analyst treats these as the same, ignoring that unknown risks cannot be weighed against benefits.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Developer's reason: the long-term impacts are unknown.
2. Analyst's attack: you use other models with known potential problems, so your stated reason must be false.
3. The gap: for other models the risks are known and can be balanced against benefits; for DeepThought the risk is unknown and cannot be balanced. That explains consistent behaviour, which option D states.

**Answer: known risks can be compared to known benefits, but unknown risks cannot**

### Why the other options are wrong
A, C and E add facts about impacts but do not explain why the developer's behaviour is consistent; B concerns benefit, not risk.

### Faster method
Look for the distinction between the two situations the analyst treated as the same (known vs unknown).

### Common traps
- Choosing C, which supports the developer's caution but does not expose the analyst's flaw.
questions.answer: known risks can be compared to known benefits, but unknown risks cannot
options: the impacts of an AI model on data integrity can sometimes take time to manifest
the AI developer could be uncertain that DeepThought has been conclusively proven to be beneficial
if left unchecked, widespread use of a defective AI model could lead to serious data integrity concerns
known risks can be compared to known benefits, but unknown risks cannot
the data impacts of DeepThought might differ from other AI models

questions.title: Logical conclusion from a passage on digital marketing and social media
questions.statement:
The passage says social media has disrupted traditional marketing models, broadened consumer touchpoints, lowered entry barriers for small businesses (causing saturation and intense competition), and created a need for new skills among groups with differential technology acceptance rates. Despite this, many enterprises remain reluctant to embrace the medium fully and supplement traditional marketing with digital channels, causing inconsistent brand messages; some theorists blame reluctance to abandon successful frameworks, others see it as a response to demographic groups with different technology acceptance.

What might be a logical conclusion that could be drawn from the passage?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0162.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0164.jpeg
questions.explanation: The passage links the blended approach to demographic groups accepting technology at different rates. A conclusion that follows is that digital strategies should serve several demographic groups. The other options go beyond the text (disregard traditional methods, small business advantage, forced adoption).
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. The passage gives two explanations for the hybrid approach; one is demographic groups with different technology acceptance.
2. A conclusion supported by that explanation: strategies should address several groups.
3. A and D and E are stronger claims not backed by the text (the passage says entry barriers fell and saturation grew, which is not an advantage; enterprises remain reluctant, so "forced" is unsupported).

**Answer: Digital marketing strategies should cater to multiple demographic groups.**

### Why the other options are wrong
A is contradicted (firms still use traditional methods); D and E overreach; C contradicts "inconsistent brand messages".

### Faster method
Choose the conclusion that restates one of the passage's own explanations, not a new claim.

### Common traps
- Selecting the option about saturation because it is mentioned in the text.
questions.answer: Digital marketing strategies should cater to multiple demographic groups.

Digital marketing strategies should cater to multiple demographic groups.
Brand messages are always consistent across channels.
Small businesses have an advantage in the digital era.
