questions.title: Airline B quarter with the biggest percentage increase
questions.statement:
A bar chart gives the number of passengers (in millions) carried by two airlines in four quarters of 2020. Airline A: Q1 15, Q2 12, Q3 18, Q4 20. Airline B: Q1 14, Q2 16, Q3 17, Q4 21.

Which quarter did Airline B see the biggest percentage increase in passengers from the previous quarter?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0059.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0061.jpeg
questions.solution:
### Solution
Percentage increase = (current - previous)/previous.
- Q2: (16-14)/14 = 14.29%
- Q3: (17-16)/16 = 6.25%
- Q4: (21-17)/17 = 23.53%
Q1 has no previous quarter in the data.

**Answer: Q4**

### Why the other options are wrong
Q2 14.3% and Q3 6.25% are lower; Q1 cannot be computed; the data are sufficient.

### Faster method
Q4 has the largest absolute rise (4) on a modest base (17), so it is the largest percentage too.

### Common traps
- Using the absolute change alone (Q2 is +2, Q4 is +4, but check the base).

questions.title: Courier company with the highest year-on-year revenue growth
questions.statement:
Annual revenue (in millions USD), 2016 to 2020. Xeon Express: 500, 550, 600, 620, 650. Paragon Couriers: 450, 520, 560, 590, 610.

Which company had the highest year-on-year revenue growth rate in any year?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0063.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0065.jpeg
questions.explanation: Paragon grew 11.1% (450 to 520) in 2017, higher than any Xeon year (best 10%, 500 to 550). Other Paragon years: 7.7%, 5.4%, 3.4%; Xeon: 9.1%, 3.3%, 4.8%.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Compute each year-on-year growth.
Xeon: 550/500 = 10.0%, 600/550 = 9.09%, 620/600 = 3.33%, 650/620 = 4.84%.
Paragon: 520/450 = 11.11%, 560/520 = 7.69%, 590/560 = 5.36%, 610/590 = 3.39%.
Highest overall = Paragon in 2017 (11.11%).

**Answer: Paragon Couriers**

### Why the other options are wrong
Xeon's best growth is 10%; the rates differ; the data are sufficient.

### Faster method
Only the first year pair can reach 10% or more: 50/450 against 50/500.

### Common traps
- Comparing absolute growth (Xeon grows by 50 in 2017 too).
options: Both had the same highest growth rate

### Solution
Let g = college graduates; non-graduates = 120 - g.
(1) 120 - g = 3g -> g = 30. Sufficient.
(2) 120 - g = g + 90 -> 2g = 30 -> g = 15. Sufficient.

### Why the other options are wrong
Each statement alone fixes g, so A, B, C and E are false.

### Faster method
Both are linear equations in one unknown, so each is sufficient.

### Common traps
- Combining the statements even though each already works.

questions.title: Data sufficiency: value of n in a five-number list
questions.statement:
n, 10, 8, 6, 12

What is the value of n in the list above?

(1) n > 12
(2) The median of the numbers in the list is 9.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Fractal\IMG-20240908-WA0088.jpeg
questions.explanation: The sorted known values are 6, 8, 10, 12. For a median of 9 with five numbers, the middle value must be n itself, between 8 and 10, so n = 9 (if n were elsewhere the median would be 8 or 10). Statement (1) gives only n > 12.
questions.solution:
### Solution
(1) n > 12 allows infinitely many values: insufficient.
(2) Five numbers, the median is the third value. With known 6, 8, 10, 12:
- n <= 8: sorted n,6/8,... median is 8.
- 8 < n < 10: sorted 6, 8, n, 10, 12, median n.
- n >= 10: median is 10.
A median of 9 therefore forces n = 9. Sufficient.

**Answer: Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.**

### Why the other options are wrong
(1) alone gives a range; the other combinations are unnecessary or wrong.

### Faster method
With an odd count, the median equals one of the values; since 9 is not in the list, it must be n.

### Common traps
- Averaging 8 and 10 as if the count were even.

questions.title: Count connected groups of people stuck after an earthquake
questions.statement: People are stuck in different parts of a city and food is to be dropped by helicopter. A "part" is a maximal 4-directionally connected group of people. Given a 2-D array city, return the number of parts. People are denoted by 0 and the rest of the city is denoted by 1.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG-20240914-WA0032.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG-20240914-WA0033.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG-20240914-WA0035.jpg
questions.explanation: Count the connected components of 0 cells under 4-direction adjacency. Scan the grid; each time an unvisited 0 is found, increment the answer and flood-fill (BFS or DFS) its component. O(N x M) time and O(N x M) space for the queue/visited marks.
questions.input_format: input1: number of rows N. input2: number of columns M. input3: N x M array, 0 = people, 1 = anything else.
questions.output_format: An integer: the number of parts.
questions.constraints: Bounds are not visible in the photographs.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
Groups of people that touch horizontally or vertically form one "part". Counting parts is exactly counting connected components of the 0 cells (this is the classic "number of islands" with 0 as land).

### Approach
1. Walk through every cell in row-major order.
2. When a cell with value 0 is found, it begins a new component: increase the counter.
3. Flood-fill the whole component with BFS, marking each reached 0 as visited (set it to 1 on a copy of the grid), moving in the four directions.
4. Continue scanning; already visited cells are skipped. The counter is the answer.

### Why it works
Each flood fill visits exactly the cells reachable from its start via 0 cells, i.e. one full component, and marks them so they are never counted again. Distinct components share no adjacent cells, so each triggers exactly one new fill.

### Complexity
O(N x M) time because every cell is pushed to the queue at most once; O(N x M) space in the worst case for the queue.

### Python solution
```python
from collections import deque

def foodDistribution(input1, input2, input3):
    n, m = input1, input2
    g = [row[:] for row in input3]      # copy so the input is not modified
    parts = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(m):
            if g[i][j] == 0:            # new, unvisited group of people
                parts += 1
                g[i][j] = 1             # mark visited
                q = deque([(i, j)])
                while q:
                    x, y = q.popleft()
                    for dx, dy in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                        a, b = x + dx, y + dy
                        if 0 <= a < n and 0 <= b < m and g[a][b] == 0:
                            g[a][b] = 1
                            q.append((a, b))
    return parts
```

### Dry run
Example 1 groups: {(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(2,1)}, {(1,3),(2,3)}, {(3,2)}, {(4,0)}, {(4,3)}. The scan meets (0,0) first (count 1, fills its component), then (1,3) (count 2), (3,2) (3), (4,0) (4), (4,3) (5). Answer 5.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Diagonal neighbours do not connect; only four directions.
- Mark cells when they are pushed, not when popped, or the same cell can be queued many times.
- A grid of all 1s returns 0; an all-0 grid returns 1.
- Use an iterative fill; recursive DFS can overflow the stack on large grids.

questions.explanation: Sort the values in descending order. An exchange argument shows an optimal partition uses groups that are contiguous in this sorted order (a larger element never sits in a lower group than a smaller one). Then dp[i] = max over j<i of dp[j] + (i-j) x (prefix[i]-prefix[j]) on the sorted array. O(N^2) time, O(N) space; verified against brute force over all set partitions.
questions.input_format: input1: N, the number of gems. input2: integer array A of gem values (may be negative).
questions.output_format: An integer: the maximum total value.
questions.constraints: Bounds are not visible in the photographs.

examples.explanation: One group {2,2}: 2 x 4 = 8.

questions.solution:
### Intuition
A group of size k and sum s is worth k x s, so putting several large positive values together multiplies their sum by the group size, while a negative value should be kept away unless it is dragged along cheaply. The groups are arbitrary subsets, so only the values matter, not the positions.

### Approach
1. Sort the values in descending order.
2. Claim: there is an optimal partition whose groups are contiguous blocks of the sorted array. Exchange argument: if a larger value x sits in a group of size p with sum S and a smaller value y sits in a group of size q with sum T where the group of x is "lower" in the ordering, swapping x and y changes the total by (q - p)(x - y) times a sign that is non-negative for a suitable orientation, so blocks never lose.
3. Let pre[i] be the sum of the first i sorted values. Define dp[i] = best total for the first i sorted values. dp[0] = 0.
4. Transition: dp[i] = max over j < i of dp[j] + (i - j) x (pre[i] - pre[j]); the last block is the sorted elements j..i-1.
5. The answer is dp[N].

### Why it works
Every partition can be rearranged without loss into contiguous blocks of the sorted order, and the DP tries every way to cut the sorted array into blocks, so it finds the best. The check script compares the DP to a brute force over all set partitions for 300 random arrays of size up to 7.

### Complexity
Sorting is O(N log N); the DP is O(N^2) time and O(N) space. If N is large the transition is a convex hull trick (dp[j] - j x pre[j] + ... lines), reducing it to O(N log N).

### Python solution
```python
def magicalGems(input1, input2):
    a = sorted(input2, reverse=True)
    n = len(a)
    pre = [0]
    for v in a:
        pre.append(pre[-1] + v)
    NEG = float('-inf')
    dp = [NEG] * (n + 1)
    dp[0] = 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(i):
            val = dp[j] + (i - j) * (pre[i] - pre[j])
            if val > dp[i]:
                dp[i] = val
    return dp[n]
```

### Dry run
Example 1: sorted = [9, 9, 2, -7], pre = [0, 9, 18, 20, 13].
dp[1] = 9, dp[2] = max(0 + 2 x 18, 9 + 9) = 36, dp[3] = max(3 x 20, 36 + 2) = 60 (one block of three), dp[4] = max(4 x 13 = 52, dp[3] + (-7) = 53, ...) = 53.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- All values negative: every element is best alone, giving the sum of values.
- A single element: its value (1 x v).
- Large sums: use 64-bit integers in other languages (the product can reach N x N x max).
- Do not assume groups must be contiguous in the original order; the sample splits 2, 9, 9 away from -7 which sits between them.
questions.notes: The task is repeated across many captures of the same question; the examples in the photographs are consistent with groups being arbitrary subsets (the sample puts 2, 9, 9 together and -7 apart).

leetcode.name: Minimum Deletions to Make Character Frequencies Unique

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Only the count of each type matters. We want distinct positive packed counts, each at most the available count of its type, with the largest possible total. This is the same idea as making character frequencies unique by deleting as little as possible.

### Approach
1. Count how many items of each type exist.
2. Sort these counts in descending order.
3. Keep `limit`, the largest value still allowed (initially infinity).
4. For each count c in order: take t = min(c, limit - 1). If t <= 0, stop (smaller counts cannot help). Otherwise add t to the answer and set limit = t.

### Why it works
Packed counts must be distinct positive integers, so if k types are used the packed counts are at most (a1, a1-1, a1-2, ...) when processed from the largest availability. Taking the largest count first and lowering each following count just enough to stay distinct never wastes capacity: if a type had to be lowered further, any other assignment would also be forced to give a smaller value to some type (exchange argument). The brute force check on 300 random cases confirms the greedy.

### Complexity
O(n log n) for counting and sorting, O(n) space.

### Python solution
```python
from collections import Counter

def maxItems(input1, input2):
    freq = sorted(Counter(input2).values(), reverse=True)
    total = 0
    limit = float('inf')          # largest count we may still use
    for f in freq:
        take = min(f, limit - 1)
        if take <= 0:
            break
        total += take
        limit = take
    return total
```

### Dry run
Example 2: counts are type 1 -> 3, type 3 -> 2, type 7 -> 2, sorted [3, 2, 2]. Take 3 (limit 3), then min(2, 2) = 2 (limit 2), then min(2, 1) = 1. Total 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Many types with equal counts: the answer is a triangular-like sum; the loop stops when `take` reaches 0.
- A single type: its entire count.
- Compare with the original array length, not with the number of types (types are values from 1 to n).

questions.solution:
### Intuition
A bench is lit when some lamp has power at least its distance to that bench. To minimise the largest power required, each bench should use its nearest lamp, and the answer is the worst such distance.

### Approach
1. Sort the lamp positions.
2. For each bench at position b, binary-search the first lamp at or after b and compare it with the previous lamp. The distance to the nearest lamp is the minimum of the two gaps.
3. The answer is the maximum nearest distance over all benches (0 if there are no benches).

### Why it works
With a uniform power P every bench is lit iff its nearest lamp is within P. The smallest such P is the maximum nearest distance, and giving each lamp only the power it needs cannot reduce the maximum below that value because the farthest bench must still be reached by some lamp. Brute force over powers 0..200 agrees on 300 random cases.

### Complexity
O(m log m) to sort the lamps and O(n log m) for the queries; O(1) extra space.

### Python solution
```python
from bisect import bisect_left

def minPower(input1, input2, input3, input4):
    lamps = sorted(input4)
    ans = 0
    for b in input3:
        i = bisect_left(lamps, b)
        d = float('inf')
        if i < len(lamps):
            d = min(d, lamps[i] - b)      # nearest lamp on the right (or at b)
        if i > 0:
            d = min(d, b - lamps[i - 1])  # nearest lamp on the left
        ans = max(ans, d)
    return ans
```

### Dry run
Example 2: lamps [5, 10, 15, 20]. Distances: bench 2 -> 3, 7 -> 2, 12 -> 2, 17 -> 2, 22 -> 2, 27 -> 7. Maximum is 7.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- A bench exactly at a lamp has distance 0 (initial power already lights it).
- Benches left of all lamps or right of all lamps use only one side.
- Duplicate lamp positions are harmless; empty bench list returns 0.
- If there are no lamps the problem is infeasible (not covered by the samples).
questions.notes: The text calls the answer the "minimum power" and the samples show different lamps raised by different amounts, but the returned value (7 in example 2, where the raises are 3, 2, 2 and 7) is the largest raise, so the problem minimises the maximum power. The first sample lists 5 bench positions while saying 6 benches.

leetcode.name: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix (4-direction variant)

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Every move costs the same, so the shortest route in a grid with blocked cells is found by breadth-first search. The path length counts cells (the entrance and the prison cell included), so the entrance has length 1.

### Approach
1. Find the cell containing 1 (entrance).
2. Run BFS from it with `dist[entrance] = 1`, moving up, down, left and right to cells that are inside the grid, not -1 and not yet seen.
3. When a popped cell holds 2, return its distance.
4. If the queue empties without reaching 2, return -1.

### Why it works
BFS processes cells in nondecreasing order of distance, so the first time the prison is dequeued its recorded distance is minimal. Soldiers are never entered, so the path avoids them.

### Complexity
O(N x M) time and space since each cell is enqueued once.

### Python solution
```python
from collections import deque

def shortestRescue(input1, input2, input3):
    n, m, g = input1, input2, input3
    start = next((i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(m) if g[i][j] == 1)
    dist = {start: 1}                       # count cells, entrance = 1
    q = deque([start])
    while q:
        x, y = q.popleft()
        if g[x][y] == 2:
            return dist[(x, y)]
        for dx, dy in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
            a, b = x + dx, y + dy
            if 0 <= a < n and 0 <= b < m and g[a][b] != -1 and (a, b) not in dist:
                dist[(a, b)] = dist[(x, y)] + 1
                q.append((a, b))
    return -1
```

### Dry run
Example 1: from (0,0) go down to (1,0) (length 2), right along row 1 to (1,3) (length 5), down to (2,3) (6) and (3,3) (7) which is the prison. Answer 7.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Length counts cells, not moves, so adjacent entrance and prison give 2.
- If the prison is walled in by soldiers return -1.
- Mark cells as seen when enqueued to avoid duplicate work.
- Cells with value 1 and 2 are both walkable; only -1 blocks.
questions.notes: The entrance marker is hidden by the cursor in the statement photo; the examples show it is 1. In example 2 the second row is read as [0,-1,-1,-1,-1] from the diagram.

In the first diagram every parent exceeds its children (95 > 63, 52; 63 > 35, 15; 52 > 45, 25; 35 > 10, 4) and levels fill left to right. The diagrams with root 63 are invalid because the child 95 is larger than the root.
questions.solution:
### Solution
A max heap needs two properties.
1. Shape: a complete binary tree (all levels full except possibly the last, filled left to right).
2. Order: every node is greater than or equal to both of its children.

Check the first diagram in level order: 95 | 63, 52 | 35, 15, 45, 25 | 10, 4. The shape is complete. Order: 95 > 63, 52; 63 > 35, 15; 52 > 45, 25; 35 > 10, 4. All hold.

The diagrams with 63 at the root have 95 as a child of 63, which breaks the order property. The second diagram shows root 95 with children 45 and 63 but the rest is cut off in the photo.

**Answer: the first diagram (root 95, children 63 and 52).**

### Why the other options are wrong
Diagrams rooted at 63 fail the order property (95 is a child of 63). The second one is only partially visible.

### Faster method
Look at the root first: in a max heap it must be the largest value in the whole tree.

### Common traps
- Checking only parent-child pairs on one branch.
- Forgetting that completeness is also required.
questions.answer: Root 95 with children 63 and 52 (the first diagram)
options: Root 63; children 45 and 95 with a different arrangement below
questions.notes: The option diagrams were photographed in pieces and options 2 to 4 are summarised; only the first diagram satisfies the heap property.

- Missing that the original array (not a copy) is sorted.

questions.explanation: Hashtable has 11 buckets, index = key mod 11, and its iterator walks buckets from the highest index to the lowest, newest entry first within a bucket. Keys map to: 9 -> 9, 5 -> 5, 1, 100 and 111 -> 1, 110 -> 0. Order: 9, 5, 111, 100, 1, 110, so the values printed are 111, 110, 9, 1, 100, 5.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Default capacity is 11, load factor 0.75 (threshold 8), so 6 entries do not trigger a rehash.
2. Bucket index = key mod 11: 1 -> 1; 100 -> 1 (100 = 9 x 11 + 1); 5 -> 5; 110 -> 0; 9 -> 9; 111 -> 1.
3. New entries are inserted at the head of a bucket chain, so bucket 1 reads 111 -> 100 -> 1.
4. The keySet iterator (an Enumerator) goes from table index 10 down to 0, following each chain.
   Order of keys: 9 (bucket 9), 5 (bucket 5), 111, 100, 1 (bucket 1), 110 (bucket 0).
5. Values printed: get(9) = 111, get(5) = 110, get(111) = 9, get(100) = 1, get(1) = 100, get(110) = 5.

**Answer: 111 110 9 1 100 5**

### Why the other options are wrong
The other options assume HashMap-style ascending order or insertion order.

### Faster method
Remember: Hashtable iterates from the last bucket to the first.

### Common traps
- Assuming insertion order (Hashtable and HashMap do not preserve it).
- Forgetting that chains put the newest entry first.

questions.title: Array state after five outer-loop iterations of insertion sort
questions.statement:
An array of 10 elements is passed through the insertion sort algorithm. What would be the resultant elements of the array obtained if the algorithm terminates exactly after five executions of the loop?

Given array: 28, 35, 12, 15, 27, 11, 9, 14, 8, 32. The sorting is in ascending order.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG_20240914_013534_730.jpg
questions.explanation: Each outer iteration inserts the next element into the sorted prefix. After five iterations the first six elements (28, 35, 12, 15, 27, 11) are sorted as 11, 12, 15, 27, 28, 35 and the last four are untouched.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Insertion sort treats the first element as a sorted prefix and inserts the elements at indices 1, 2, 3, ... in turn.
- After step 1 (insert 35): 28 35 12 15 27 11 9 14 8 32
- Step 2 (12): 12 28 35 15 27 11 ...
- Step 3 (15): 12 15 28 35 27 11 ...
- Step 4 (27): 12 15 27 28 35 11 ...
- Step 5 (11): 11 12 15 27 28 35 9 14 8 32
The remaining elements 9, 14, 8, 32 are untouched.

**Answer: 11 12 15 27 28 35 9 14 8 32**

### Why the other options are wrong
The first and second options stop after 2 and 4 steps; the fourth has already inserted 9 (a sixth step).

### Faster method
After k steps the first k+1 elements are sorted and the rest unchanged.

### Common traps
- Counting the first element as a step (that gives the 4-step result).
questions.notes: Counts one outer-loop execution as one insertion step starting from index 1, so five steps sort the first six elements.

questions.title: Possible insertion order for a linear-probing hash table
questions.statement: Consider a hash table with hash function h(k) = k mod 10 that uses linear probing for collision resolution. Suppose the keys 26, 22, 24, 32, 33, 23 are inserted into the empty table in some order and the final state is: index 2: 22, index 3: 33, index 4: 24, index 5: 32, index 6: 26, index 7: 23. What is the correct order in which the values could have been inserted?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG_20240914_013534_731.jpg
questions.explanation: Simulate the order 26, 24, 22, 33, 32, 23: 26 goes to 6, 24 to 4, 22 to 2, 33 to 3, 32 collides at 2, 3, 4 and lands in 5, 23 collides at 3, 4, 5, 6 and lands in 7, which matches the table.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Test each order by simulating linear probing.
1. 22, 33, 32, 23, 26, 24: 22 -> 2, 33 -> 3, 32 -> 2 taken, 3 taken, so 4 (but the target layout has 24 at 4). Fails.
2. 32, 23, 22, 33, 26, 24: 32 goes to 2, but the table has 22 at 2. Fails.
3. 26, 24, 22, 33, 32, 23: 26 -> 6; 24 -> 4; 22 -> 2; 33 -> 3; 32 -> 2, 3, 4 taken, so 5; 23 -> 3, 4, 5, 6 taken, so 7. Matches the table.
4. 22, 32, 26, 24, 23, 33: 32 would go to 3 (2 taken), but the table has 33 at 3. Fails.

**Answer: 26, 24, 22, 33, 32, 23**

### Why the other options are wrong
See the failure points in 1, 2 and 4.

### Faster method
Keys sitting away from their home slot (32 at 5, 23 at 7) must have been inserted after the keys that block them (22, 33, 24 and 26).

### Common traps
- Forgetting that probing wraps over occupied slots one at a time.

questions.title: Missing step when removing the last node of a singly linked list
questions.statement: You are working on a project involving a linked list data structure. The project requires you to implement a method to remove the last element of the linked list. You have implemented the method, but after running some tests, you notice it is not working as expected. The last element is not being removed from the list. After reviewing your code, you realize you missed a crucial step. What step did you forget to implement?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG_20240914_013534_807.jpg
questions.explanation: In a singly linked list you can only remove the last node by changing the next pointer of the second last node to null. Without traversing to the second last element, the last node stays linked.
questions.solution:
### Solution
A singly linked list node knows only its successor. To delete the tail you must set `secondLast.next = null` (and update the tail pointer if one is kept). The second last node is found by walking until `node.next.next == null`.

**Answer: Traverse to the second last element before removing the last element.**

### Why the other options are wrong
The third or fourth last node is not adjacent to the tail, so its next pointer cannot detach the last node; the first element is the head, which is only right for a one-element list.

### Faster method
To delete a node you always need its predecessor.

### Common traps
- Moving the tail pointer without clearing the previous node's next field.

questions.title: Binary search for the first missing element in a sorted list
questions.statement: A sorted list of ten numbers is given as A = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10]. The requirement is to find the first missing element index; in this case 7 is the missing element. Select the correct binary search algorithm for the above requirement.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG_20240914_013534_808.jpg
questions.explanation: Before the missing value, A[i] == i; from the missing value onward, A[i] > i. Compare the middle value with its index: equal means the gap is on the right, different means the gap is at or to the left of the middle. Repeat to narrow down.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Observation: for i before the missing value, A[i] = i. At and after the first missing value, A[i] = i + 1 (here), so A[i] > i.
1. Compare A[mid] with mid. If equal, all elements up to mid are in place, so the missing value is on the right.
2. If different, the missing value is at mid or on the left, so move left.
3. The search must repeat on the reduced range until the range has one element. Here A[7] = 8 != 7, so the first missing value is 7 at index 7.

The last option states these steps and includes the repeat step. The third option omits the repeat, so it is only one comparison, not a binary search.

**Answer: the last option (compare middle value and middle index, right if same, left if different, repeat, return the index).**

### Why the other options are wrong
Options 1 and 2 split the list without comparing the middle value to its index (option 2 also never defines the comparison); option 3 does not repeat.

### Faster method
The loop invariant "A[i] == i on the left side" is the key; everything else follows.

### Common traps
- Searching for the value instead of using value-index equality.

questions.title: Worst case of insertion in a binary search tree
questions.statement:
Given are two statements about the insertion operation in a binary search tree. Which of these is/are correct?
A) The worst case happens when the given keys are sorted in ascending or descending order.
B) The worst case happens when all the nodes except the leaf have one and only one child.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG_20240914_013535_347.jpg
questions.explanation: Sorted keys make a skewed (linked-list) tree, and in a skewed tree every non-leaf node has exactly one child. Both describe the same worst case, where each insertion takes O(n).
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Inserting keys in ascending order always goes right, descending always goes left. The tree becomes a chain of height n, and each insertion walks the whole chain: O(n).
2. A chain is exactly a tree where every node except the leaf has one child, so statement B is the structural description of the same worst case. (A tree with one-child nodes in zig-zag order is also height n, so B is a valid worst-case shape.)
Both statements are correct.

**Answer: Both A and B**

### Why the other options are wrong
Only A or Only B each leave out a correct statement; Neither is false.

### Faster method
Worst case for a BST = height n = skewed tree.

### Common traps
- Thinking B is wrong because the chain does not go in one direction; any one-child-per-node shape has height n.

questions.title: Call-stack depth for a tail-recursive factorial with tail-call optimisation
questions.statement: Assuming f(n) is a function that returns the factorial of a number n, if f(n) is implemented recursively and the compiler is capable of optimizing tail recursion, what would be the maximum depth of the call stack, at any given time, created by the call f(10)?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG_20240914_013534_617.jpg
questions.explanation: With tail-call optimisation the compiler reuses the same stack frame for each recursive call, so the call stack depth stays at 1.
questions.solution:
### Solution
A tail call is a call that is the last action of the function, so its caller's frame is no longer needed. A compiler that optimises tail calls replaces the call by a jump and reuses the frame, turning the recursion into a loop. The depth therefore stays at one frame for f(10).
Without optimisation the depth would be 10 (or 11 with the base case call).

**Answer: 1**

### Why the other options are wrong
10 and 11 are the depths without optimisation; 2 would need an extra permanent frame.

### Faster method
TCO means O(1) stack space.

### Common traps
- Counting n frames out of habit.
questions.notes: The question assumes the factorial is written in tail-recursive form (with an accumulator).

questions.title: Syllogism: giraffes, short and dogs
questions.statement:
Two statements are given, followed by two conclusions. Assuming the statements to be true, decide which conclusion logically follows, disregarding commonly known facts.

All giraffe are short. All short are dogs.
Conclusion 1: Some giraffe are dogs.
Conclusion 2: Some dogs are short.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG-20240914-WA0036.jpg
questions.explanation: All giraffe are short and all short are dogs, so all giraffe are dogs, which implies some giraffe are dogs. "All short are dogs" also implies some dogs are short (the converse of an A statement gives an I statement when the class is non-empty).
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Giraffe ⊂ Short ⊂ Dogs, so Giraffe ⊂ Dogs. "All giraffe are dogs" gives "Some giraffe are dogs": conclusion 1 follows.
2. "All short are dogs" gives "Some dogs are short" by conversion (the subset is non-empty): conclusion 2 follows.

**Answer: Both conclusions follow**

### Why the other options are wrong
Dropping either conclusion ignores a valid inference.

### Faster method
Draw nested circles: giraffe inside short inside dogs.

### Common traps
- Treating "some dogs are short" as unsupported because the statement says "all short are dogs" (the converse of an A statement is I).

questions.statement: In a certain coding system, 'TEN' is coded as 256 and 'SIXTY' is coded as 19827. How will you code 'SIXTEEN'?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sigmoid\IMG-20240914-WA0039.jpg
questions.explanation: From TEN = 256: T = 2, E = 5, N = 6. From SIXTY = 19827: S = 1, I = 9, X = 8, T = 2, Y = 7. So SIXTEEN = S I X T E E N = 1 9 8 2 5 5 6 = 1982556.
questions.solution:

Match letters with digits position by position.

- SIXTY -> 1, 9, 8, 2, 7 gives S = 1, I = 9, X = 8, T = 2 (consistent with TEN), Y = 7.
- SIXTEEN = S, I, X, T, E, E, N = 1, 9, 8, 2, 5, 5, 6.

**Answer: 1982556**

### Faster method
Write a letter-to-digit table and read off the word.

- Forgetting that E repeats.

Look at consecutive ratios and differences: 7 -> 21 (x3), 21 -> 22 (+1), 22 -> 66 (x3), 66 -> 67 (+1), 67 -> ? (x3) = 201, 201 -> 202 (+1), 202 -> 606 (x3). The pattern repeats, so the missing term is 201.

source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0029.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0031.jpeg
questions.explanation: Each word equals twice its number of letters: LAMENT (6) -> 12, SOFTENS (7) -> 14, so SCAM (4) -> 8.
questions.solution:
### Solution
LAMENT has 6 letters and is 12; SOFTENS has 7 letters and is 14; the value is 2 x (number of letters). SCAM has 4 letters, so 8.

**Answer: 8**

### Why the other options are wrong
18, 12 and 6 do not equal 2 x 4.

### Faster method
Compare number of letters with the value.

questions.title: Syllogism: no horses are molluscs and all crabs are horses
questions.statement: Statements: I. No horses are molluscs. II. All crabs are horses. Which conclusion follows?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0031.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0033.jpeg
questions.explanation: Crabs lie inside horses, and horses have no overlap with molluscs, so crabs have none either.
questions.solution:
### Solution
All crabs are horses, so crabs are a subset of horses. No horse is a mollusc, so no crab is a mollusc. "Some horses are not crabs" cannot be inferred (all horses could be crabs).

**Answer: No crabs are molluscs**

### Why the other options are wrong
"All molluscs are crabs" contradicts statement I; "Some horses are not crabs" is possible but not certain.

### Faster method
A-statement followed by an E-statement gives an E conclusion.

questions.title: Eight friends by height: taller than Oliver and from the same city
questions.statement:
Eight friends Oliver, John, Ethan, Oscar, Bruce, Jonathan, Harry and Kevin are of different heights and stand in a row facing North in decreasing order of height from left to right (shortest at the extreme right). Three are from Mumbai, three from Paris and the rest from New York.
I. Kevin, the 2nd tallest, is not from Mumbai and Harry, the 4th tallest, is from Paris.
II. Oscar is from Paris but Jonathan is not from New York.
III. Oliver is taller than John but shorter than Harry, while Bruce is shorter than Kevin.
IV. Jonathan is shorter than John but taller than Ethan.
V. Neither the shortest nor the second shortest friend is from Mumbai.

Who among the following is taller than Oliver and is also from the same city as him?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0033.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0035.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0037.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0137.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0138.jpg
questions.explanation: The order is Oscar, Kevin, Bruce, Harry, Oliver, John, Jonathan, Ethan. Cities: Paris - Oscar, Harry, Jonathan; Mumbai - Bruce, Oliver, John; New York - Kevin, Ethan. Bruce is from Mumbai like Oliver and taller than him.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Kevin is 2nd and Harry 4th. Oliver < Harry, John < Oliver, Jonathan < John, Ethan < Jonathan, so positions 5 to 8 are Oliver, John, Jonathan, Ethan.
2. Oscar and Bruce take positions 1 and 3; Bruce is shorter than Kevin, so Bruce is 3rd and Oscar is 1st.
3. Cities: Harry, Oscar are Paris. Shortest (Ethan) and second shortest (Jonathan) are not Mumbai; Jonathan is not New York, so Jonathan is Paris (third Paris person). Ethan is then New York; Kevin (not Mumbai, Paris full) is New York. The remaining three, Bruce, Oliver and John, are from Mumbai.
4. Taller than Oliver and Mumbai: Bruce (position 3). John is shorter.

A computer search of all 40,320 orderings confirms this is the only arrangement.

**Answer: Bruce**

### Why the other options are wrong
Oscar is from Paris; Jonathan is from Paris and shorter; John is from Mumbai but shorter than Oliver.

questions.title: Flowchart behaviour on an empty file
questions.statement: A flowchart prints "Name" and "Total", sets ctr = 0, reads Name and Amount, then tests End Of File. If End Of File is true it prints "Number of records read" with ctr and stops; otherwise it sets Namebreak = "No", Old Name = Name, Total = 0, prints Name and processes the group (more steps not visible). How will the flowchart handle a scenario where the file is empty?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0056.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0058.jpeg
questions.explanation: On an empty file the first read hits End Of File immediately, so the flow goes straight to "Print Number of records read ctr" with ctr = 0 and then stops.
questions.solution:
### Solution
The header line is printed first, then ctr = 0, then the first read finds nothing and the End Of File decision is true. The true branch prints the record count (still 0) and stops. No error and no loop occur.

**Answer: There will be no error and it prints "Number of records read" as zero**

### Why the other options are wrong
Nothing is printed only if the stop did not print the count; the loop is never entered.

### Common traps
- Forgetting that the header is printed before the first read.
questions.answer: There will be no error and it prints "Number of records read" as zero
options: The flow chart will throw an error
There will be no error and it will not print anything
This will get into an infinite loop
There will be no error and it prints "Number of records read" as zero
questions.notes: Only the upper half of the flowchart is visible in the photographs.

questions.title: Six presentations: number of possible schedules
questions.statement:
Six persons Jacob, William, Liam, Alexander, Ethan and Andrew give presentations, not necessarily in this order.
I. Andrew delivers either at the start or at the end.
II. Jacob delivers immediately after Ethan.
III. There are exactly three presentations between William and Liam.
IV. Alexander is the second person to deliver.

How many different possible scheduling combinations are possible?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0058.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0060.jpeg
questions.explanation: Alexander is 2nd, so William and Liam must be 1st and 5th (three between them). Andrew must then be 6th, leaving Ethan 3rd and Jacob 4th. William and Liam can swap, giving 2 schedules.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Positions 1 to 6. Alexander = 2. The pairs of positions with exactly three people between are (1,5) and (2,6); position 2 is taken, so William and Liam use 1 and 5 in either order.
Andrew must be first or last; 1 is taken, so Andrew is 6. Jacob follows Ethan directly in the free positions 3 and 4: Ethan 3, Jacob 4.
Two schedules: William, Alexander, Ethan, Jacob, Liam, Andrew and Liam, Alexander, Ethan, Jacob, William, Andrew. A brute-force search over all 720 orders gives the same two.

**Answer: 2**

### Why the other options are wrong
1, 3 and 4 miscount the swap of William and Liam.

questions.title: Six presentations: who delivers immediately after William
questions.statement: In the schedule problem where Andrew presents first or last, Jacob follows Ethan, exactly three presentations lie between William and Liam, and Alexander is second: who delivers his presentation immediately after William?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0060.jpeg
questions.explanation: In the two valid schedules, William is either 1st (followed by Alexander) or 5th (followed by Andrew).
questions.solution:
### Solution
Schedule 1: William, Alexander, Ethan, Jacob, Liam, Andrew -> after William comes Alexander. Schedule 2: Liam, Alexander, Ethan, Jacob, William, Andrew -> after William comes Andrew. Both schedules are valid, so the answer is "either".

**Answer: Either Alexander or Andrew**

### Why the other options are wrong
Jacob never directly follows William; a single name would be wrong in one schedule.

questions.title: Probability that a box with 3 defective articles passes the sampling test
questions.statement: Out of a set of 15 articles, 3 are chosen at random. If any one of them is found to be defective, then the whole set is put under 100% screening. If no item is found to be defective, it is sent for sale. Find the probability that a box containing 3 defective articles will be sent for the sale.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0062.jpeg
questions.explanation: The box is sold only when all 3 chosen items are good: C(12,3)/C(15,3) = 220/455 = 44/91.
questions.solution:
### Solution
There are 12 good articles. P(all three chosen good) = C(12,3)/C(15,3) = 220/455 = 44/91.

**Answer: 44/91**

### Why the other options are wrong
52/91 and 9/91 do not equal 220/455; 88/91 is 2 x 44/91.

### Faster method
(12/15)(11/14)(10/13) = 1320/2730 = 44/91.

questions.title: Value of a ratio of powers of 6, 8, 2 and 3
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0062.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0156.jpg
questions.explanation: Powers: numerator 6^8 x 8^10 x 2^6 x 3^4, denominator 6^6 x 8^12 x 3^6. The ratio is 6^2 x 8^-2 x 2^6 x 3^-2 = 36 x 64 / (64 x 9) = 4.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Numerator: (6^4)^2 = 6^8, (8^5)^2 = 8^10, (2^2)^3 = 2^6, (3^2)^2 = 3^4. Denominator: (6^2)^3 = 6^6, (8^3)^4 = 8^12, (3^3)^2 = 3^6.
Ratio = 6^(8-6) x 8^(10-12) x 2^6 x 3^(4-6) = 36 / 64 x 64 / 9 = 4.

**Answer: 4**

### Why the other options are wrong
The other options come from sign errors in the exponents.

### Faster method
Cancel like bases first: 6^2 / 3^2 = 4 and 2^6 / 8^2 = 1.

questions.title: Maximum possible sum of the A.P. 40, 36, 32, ...
questions.statement: The maximum possible sum of the A.P. series 40, 36, 32, ... is:
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0062.jpeg
questions.explanation: The terms are 40, 36, ..., 4, 0 (11 terms), after which they turn negative. Sum = 11/2 x (40 + 0) = 220.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Terms are positive until 40 - 4(n-1) = 0, i.e. n = 11 (the 11th term is 0). The maximum sum is S = 11 x (40 + 0)/2 = 220; adding negative terms only reduces it.

**Answer: 220**

### Why the other options are wrong
225 and 232 would need positive terms beyond zero; 320 is the sum of 40 terms without stopping.

### Common traps
- Continuing the series into negative terms.

questions.title: Value of a for divisibility by x^2 + 1
questions.statement: What is the value of a when 3x^4 + 4x^3 + 5x^2 + 4x + a is divisible by x^2 + 1?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0064.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0155.jpg
questions.solution:
### Solution
Divide: 3x^4 + 4x^3 + 5x^2 + 4x + a = (x^2 + 1)(3x^2 + 4x + 2) + (a - 2). For divisibility the remainder a - 2 must be 0, so a = 2.
Check with x = i: 3 - 4i - 5 + 4i + a = a - 2 = 0.

**Answer: 2**

### Why the other options are wrong
Any other value leaves a nonzero remainder a - 2.

### Faster method
Substitute x^2 = -1: 3 - 5 + a + (4x^3 + 4x = 4x(x^2 + 1) = 0) = a - 2.

questions.title: Angle PRQ in a right triangle with hypotenuse twice a leg
questions.statement: In triangle PQR, angle QPR is a right angle and QR is twice the length of PQ. The measure of angle PRQ is:
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0064.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0158.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0159.jpg
questions.explanation: QR is the hypotenuse and PQ = QR/2, so sin(PRQ) = PQ/QR = 1/2 and angle PRQ = 30 degrees.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Angle P = 90 degrees, so QR is the hypotenuse. The side opposite angle R is PQ, so sin R = PQ / QR = 1/2, giving R = 30 degrees.

**Answer: 30 degrees**

### Why the other options are wrong
60 degrees is angle Q; 45 and 75 degrees need other side ratios.

questions.title: Speed of a bus from a given velocity law and acceleration
questions.statement: A bus begins moving at time t = 0 and 3 seconds after the beginning attains an acceleration of 2 m/s^2. Find the speed of the bus 6 seconds after the beginning if the speed varies according to v(t) = t^2 + 2kt + 4 (m/s), where k is a constant. The object moves along a straight line.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0064.jpeg
questions.explanation: Acceleration is dv/dt = 2t + 2k. At t = 3 it is 6 + 2k = 2, so k = -2. Then v(6) = 36 - 24 + 4 = 16 m/s.
questions.solution:
### Solution
a(t) = dv/dt = 2t + 2k. a(3) = 6 + 2k = 2 gives k = -2. v(t) = t^2 - 4t + 4 = (t - 2)^2, so v(6) = 16 m/s.

**Answer: 16 m/s**

### Why the other options are wrong
25 would be v(7); 12 and "cannot be determined" ignore that k is fixed by the acceleration data.

### Faster method
v = (t - 2)^2, so v(6) = 4^2.

questions.title: Cylinder: x added to radius or height gives the same volume increase
questions.statement: Consider a cylinder with a diameter of its base as 20 cm and height 4 cm. If x cm is added to either the radius or the height to get the same increase in the volume of the cylinder, then the value of x is:
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0066.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0155.jpg
questions.explanation: With r = 10 and h = 4: pi[(10 + x)^2 x 4 - 400] = pi[100 x (4 + x) - 400], which simplifies to 4x^2 = 20x, so x = 5.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Increase from the radius: pi x 4 x [(10 + x)^2 - 100] = pi x 4 x (20x + x^2).
Increase from the height: pi x 100 x x.
Equate: 4(20x + x^2) = 100x, so 4x^2 - 20x = 0 and x = 5 (x = 0 is trivial).

**Answer: 5**

### Why the other options are wrong
16, 25 and 4 do not satisfy 4x^2 = 20x.

### Faster method
Test x = 5: 4(100 + 25) = 500 = 100 x 5.

questions.title: Number of trailing zeros in 963 factorial
questions.statement: Find the number of zeroes in 963!. (Printed options: 223, 237, 246, 251.)
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0066.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0147.jpg
questions.explanation: Count factors of 5: floor(963/5) = 192, floor(963/25) = 38, floor(963/125) = 7, floor(963/625) = 1. Total 238.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Trailing zeros = number of factors of 5 (2s are plentiful): 192 + 38 + 7 + 1 = 238.
None of the printed options (223, 237, 246, 251) equals 238, so the exam item or the option list is likely misprinted; the closest is 237.

**Answer: 238**

### Faster method
Divide repeatedly by 5 and add the quotients.

### Common traps
- Stopping after the first division (192).
questions.notes: The correct value 238 is not among the printed options, so the original item has a discrepancy.

questions.title: Number of zeroes at the end of a product
questions.statement: Find the number of zeroes in the result of 5 x 15 x 22 x 11 x 44 x 135 x 20 x 42 x 95.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0066.jpeg
questions.explanation: Factors of 5: 5, 15, 135, 20 and 95 give five 5s. Factors of 2: 22, 44 (two), 20 (two) and 42 give six 2s. Zeros = min(5, 6) = 5.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Count the primes 2 and 5. 5s: 5 (1), 15 (1), 135 (1), 20 (1), 95 (1) = 5. 2s: 22 (1), 44 (2), 20 (2), 42 (1) = 6. Each trailing zero needs one 2 and one 5, so there are min(5, 6) = 5 zeros.

**Answer: 5**

### Why the other options are wrong
Smaller counts forget some multiples of 5; 5 is the min of the two prime counts.

### Common traps
- Counting only numbers ending in 0 or 5 (the 5s appear in 135 and 95 as well).

questions.title: Total income of A from ratios of total and fixed income
questions.statement: The total incomes of A and B are in the ratio 2 : 3 when each of them has earned a variable of $300. Determine A's total income if the ratio of their fixed incomes is 1 : 2.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0066.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0068.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0160.jpg
questions.explanation: Let fixed incomes be a and 2a: (a + 300)/(2a + 300) = 2/3, so 3a + 900 = 4a + 600, a = 300. A's total is 300 + 300 = 600.
questions.solution:
### Solution
(a + 300) : (2a + 300) = 2 : 3 gives 3a + 900 = 4a + 600, so a = 300. A's total income = fixed 300 + variable 300 = $600.

**Answer: $600**

### Why the other options are wrong
$300 is only A's fixed income; $400 and $350 do not satisfy the ratio.

### Faster method
Test $600: A = 600, B = 900, ratio 2:3.

questions.title: Delay if no additional workers had been employed
questions.statement: Matt wants to build his dream house in 70 days. He employed 40 workers in the beginning and 50 more workers after 34 days to complete the work. Find the delay (in days) if no additional workers would have been employed.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0068.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0148.jpg
questions.explanation: Total work = 40 x 34 + 90 x 36 = 4600 worker-days. With only 40 workers it takes 115 days, a delay of 45 days.
questions.solution:
### Solution
The house was finished on time with 40 workers for 34 days and 90 workers for the remaining 36 days: 1360 + 3240 = 4600 worker-days. With 40 workers alone: 4600 / 40 = 115 days. Delay = 115 - 70 = 45 days.

**Answer: 45**

### Why the other options are wrong
30, 39 and 40 come from using 50 workers instead of 90 after day 34.

### Common traps
- Using 50 instead of 40 + 50 = 90 workers after day 34.

questions.title: Amount spent on emergency funds
questions.statement: Monty's monthly income is $4000. He spends 36% of his income on rent, 25% on food, 30% on investment and the rest on emergency funds. What is the amount (in $) that he spends on emergency funds?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0068.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0149.jpg
questions.solution:
### Solution
Remaining percentage = 100 - (36 + 25 + 30) = 9%. 9% of 4000 = 360.

**Answer: 360**

### Why the other options are wrong
450 is 11.25%, 499 and 299 are not 9%.

questions.title: Custom operations: (6#2)@(51?43)
questions.statement: Read the information given below. x#y = (x^3 - y^3), x?y = (x - y), x@y = x / y. Determine the value of [(6#2) @ (51?43)].
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0071.jpeg
questions.solution:
### Solution
6#2 = 6^3 - 2^3 = 208. 51?43 = 51 - 43 = 8. 208 @ 8 = 208 / 8 = 26.

**Answer: 26**

### Why the other options are wrong
52 and 13 are 208/4 and 208/16.

### Faster method
Evaluate the brackets first.
questions.notes: The other version of the paper uses different operators for a similar item (see the next question).

questions.title: Custom operations: (52$2)&(24?16)
questions.statement: Read the information given below. x?y = (x + y)/2, x&y = (x^2 - y^2), x$y = (x - y)/2. Determine the value of [(52$2) & (24?16)].
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0157.jpg
questions.solution:
### Solution
52$2 = (52 - 2)/2 = 25. 24?16 = (24 + 16)/2 = 20. 25 & 20 = 25^2 - 20^2 = 625 - 400 = 225.

**Answer: 225**

### Why the other options are wrong
25 and 125 are intermediate values; the result is 225.

### Faster method
25^2 - 20^2 = (25 - 20)(25 + 20) = 5 x 45.

questions.title: Product of F, G and H for a = 2, b = -3
questions.statement: F(a, b) = |a - b|, G(a, b) = -F(a, b), H(a, b) = |a + b|. If a = 2 and b = -3, what is the value of F.G.H?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0071.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0158.jpg
questions.solution:
### Solution
F(2, -3) = |2 - (-3)| = 5. G = -5. H = |2 + (-3)| = 1. Product = 5 x (-5) x 1 = -25.

**Answer: -25**

### Why the other options are wrong
36 is (a - b)^2 + ... not applicable; positive 25 forgets the sign of G.

### Common traps
- Forgetting the negative sign in G.

questions.title: Time for an 80 m train at 54 km/h to pass a building
questions.statement: A 80 m long train is running at a speed of 54 kmph and passes a building. What is the time taken by the train to pass by the building?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0073.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0156.jpg
questions.explanation: 54 km/h = 15 m/s, and the train must cover its own length: 80 / 15 = 5.33 s.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Speed = 54 x 5/18 = 15 m/s. The distance to pass a building is the train length: 80 m. Time = 80 / 15 = 5.33 s, i.e. 5.3 s.

**Answer: 5.3 seconds**

### Why the other options are wrong
8 s would be 120 m; 9 s would be 135 m; 4.5 s would be 67.5 m.

### Faster method
54 kmph = 15 m/s; 80/15.

questions.title: Overall percentage change of infrastructure expenditure of five countries
questions.statement:
A bar chart gives infrastructure expenditure (million $) of five countries. 2013-2014: US 830, France 750, Scotland 750, UK 1075, India 720. 2012-2013: US 1100, France 900, Scotland 720, UK 1150, India 965.

Calculate the percentage change in the overall infrastructure expenditure of the five countries together between 2012-2013 and 2013-2014.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0073.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0075.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0149.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0150.jpg
questions.solution:
### Solution
2012-2013 total: 1100 + 900 + 720 + 1150 + 965 = 4835. 2013-2014 total: 830 + 750 + 750 + 1075 + 720 = 4125. Change = -710 / 4835 = -14.68%.

**Answer: 14.68 %**

### Why the other options are wrong
The other options do not equal 710/4835.

### Common traps
- Using 2013-14 as the base (gives 17.2%).
questions.notes: The chart labels in the photograph are slightly blurry; the figures are consistent with the offered answer.

questions.title: Syllogism: boots, jugs, plastics, cars and vehicles
questions.statement:
Statements: I. Some boots are jugs. II. All jugs are plastics. III. Some plastics are cars. IV. All cars are vehicles.
Conclusions: I. Some plastics are boots. II. Some plastics are cars. III. Some vehicles are plastics.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0121.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0122.jpg
questions.explanation: I follows from I and II (some boots are jugs, all jugs are plastics). II repeats statement III. III follows from III and IV.
questions.solution:
### Solution
1. Some boots are jugs and all jugs are plastics, so some boots are plastics, and by conversion some plastics are boots (conclusion I).
2. Conclusion II is statement III itself.
3. Some plastics are cars and all cars are vehicles, so those plastics are vehicles: some vehicles are plastics (conclusion III).

**Answer: All follow**

### Why the other options are wrong
Each other option omits a valid conclusion.
options: Only conclusions I and II follow

questions.title: Number of terms of an A.P. with sum 72
questions.statement: The sum of a series in A.P. is 72, the first term is 17 and the common difference is -2. What is the number of terms in the series?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0146.jpg
questions.solution:
### Solution
S_n = n/2 [2 x 17 + (n - 1)(-2)] = n(18 - n). Set it to 72: n^2 - 18n + 72 = 0, giving (n - 6)(n - 12) = 0. Both are valid because the series goes negative after the 9th term and cancels.

**Answer: 6 or 12**

### Why the other options are wrong
6 or 13 and 8 or 12 do not satisfy the quadratic.

### Common traps
- Giving only one root.

questions.title: Time to avert a head-on collision between two trains
questions.statement: Ohio Express starts from Ohio at 6:30 a.m. and travels at 50 kmph towards Toronto situated 100 km away. At 7:00 a.m., Vancouver-Ohio Express leaves Toronto towards Ohio and travels at 40 kmph. At 7:30 a.m., Mr. Sundar, the traffic inspector at Toronto, realizes that both the trains are running on the same track. How much time does he have to avert a head-on collision between the two trains?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0148.jpg
questions.explanation: By 7:30 the first train has gone 50 km and the second 20 km, leaving 30 km. Closing speed 90 km/h, so 30/90 h = 20 minutes.
questions.solution:
### Solution
At 7:30 a.m.: train 1 travelled 1 h x 50 = 50 km; train 2 travelled 0.5 h x 40 = 20 km. Gap = 100 - 50 - 20 = 30 km. Relative speed = 50 + 40 = 90 km/h. Time = 30/90 h = 1/3 h = 20 minutes.

**Answer: 20 minutes**

### Why the other options are wrong
15, 25 and 30 minutes come from wrong gap or speed sums.

### Common traps
- Forgetting that train 2 started 30 minutes after train 1.

questions.title: Probability of exactly 3 chocolates in the first of 3 bags
questions.statement: Amanda keeps 8 identical chocolates in 3 similar bags at random. What is the probability that she kept exactly 3 chocolates in the first bag?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Procdna\IMG-20240820-WA0159.jpg
questions.explanation: Each chocolate independently goes to the first bag with probability 1/3: P = C(8,3)(1/3)^3(2/3)^5 = 56 x 32 / 6561 = 0.2731.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Treat each of the 8 chocolates as placed independently and uniformly in one of 3 bags (the intended model, since it matches an option). Exactly 3 in the first bag: C(8,3) x (1/3)^3 x (2/3)^5 = 56 x 32 / 6561 = 0.2731.

**Answer: 0.2731**

### Why the other options are wrong
The other options do not match the binomial value.
questions.notes: If the bags were filled uniformly over compositions of 8 into 3 parts (45 equally likely), the probability would be 6/45 = 0.133, which is not an option, so the independent-placement model is the intended one.

questions.title: Max heap built from 3 5 8 88 6 45 and then inserting 50
questions.statement: Construct a max heap from the values 3, 5, 8, 88, 6, 45 (inserting them in the given order). Which statement is true when 50 is inserted into the resultant heap?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_162253897_HDR_AE.jpg
questions.explanation: Inserting one by one gives [88, 8, 45, 3, 6, 5]. Adding 50 at the end and sifting up past 45 gives [88, 8, 50, 3, 6, 5, 45], so 8 and 50 are the two children of 88.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Insert one at a time with sift-up: 3 -> [3]; 5 -> [5,3]; 8 -> [8,3,5]; 88 -> [88,8,5,3]; 6 -> [88,8,5,3,6]; 45 -> [88,8,45,3,6,5].
Insert 50 at index 6 (child of index 2 = 45): 50 > 45 so swap: [88, 8, 50, 3, 6, 5, 45]. 50 < 88 stops.
Tree: root 88; children 8 and 50; 8 has 3, 6; 50 has 5, 45.
- Height is 2 (7 nodes), not 3.
- 8 is internal, so "3, 8, 5, 45 are leaves" is false.
- 8 and 50 are siblings: true.
- 5 is a leaf, so "88, 8, 5, 50 are internal" is false.

**Answer: Sibling of 8 is 50.**

### Why the other options are wrong
See the node-by-node checks above.

### Common traps
- Using bottom-up heapify instead of insertion changes the shape.
options: Height of heap is 3 (if root is at height 0)
3, 8, 5 and 45 will be the leaf nodes.
questions.notes: Assumes the heap is built by repeated insertion; a bottom-up heapify would give a different layout.

questions.title: Condition for an empty circular linked list with a tail pointer
questions.statement: Consider a circular linked list L (nodes 3, 7, 45, 90, with head pointing to node 3 and the last node pointing back). Which option is used to indicate L is empty, if current is a pointer to the last node?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_162325628_HDR_AE.jpg
questions.explanation: When the list is addressed through a pointer to its last node, an empty list is signalled by that pointer being NULL.
questions.solution:
### Solution
In a circular list the last node points to the first, so keeping only a pointer to the last node is enough to reach both ends. The list is empty exactly when this pointer is NULL. current == head is true for a single node, not an empty list.

**Answer: current == NULL**

### Why the other options are wrong
head == NULL is meaningful only if head is the pointer being kept; current == head holds for a one-node list.

questions.explanation: Each vertex of a complete graph on n vertices is joined to the other n-1.
questions.solution:
### Solution
In a complete graph every pair of vertices is adjacent, so each vertex has degree n-1. A queue is used for BFS, not to represent a graph; a regular graph needs every vertex to have the same degree (both in and out for directed graphs).

**Answer: In a complete graph, the degree of each vertex is n-1.**

### Why the other options are wrong
Option 1 confuses representation with BFS; option 3 requires only in-degree equality, which is not the definition.

questions.title: What does the pseudocode compute on a square matrix
questions.statement: Find(mat, size): flag = 1; for i = 0..size-1, for j = 0..size-1: if i = j and mat[i][j] != 1 then flag = 0, break; if i != j and mat[i][j] != 0 then flag = 0, break. After the loops, if flag = 1 write("Output"). What does the algorithm do?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_162439435_HDR_AE.jpg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_162447923_HDR_AE.jpg
questions.explanation: It requires all diagonal entries to be 1 and all off-diagonal entries to be 0, which defines the identity (unit) matrix.
questions.solution:
### Solution
The flag is cleared if a diagonal entry is not 1 or an off-diagonal entry is not 0. "Output" is written only if every diagonal entry is 1 and every other entry is 0: the identity matrix. A scalar matrix would allow any equal diagonal value; a zero matrix needs all zeros.

**Answer: Finds whether the given matrix is a unit matrix or not.**

### Why the other options are wrong
Scalar allows other diagonal values, zero needs all zeros, singular is about the determinant.

### Common traps
- The break only exits the inner loop, but flag stays 0.

questions.title: Blood relation from a coded expression M % N & O $ P & Q @ S
questions.statement: X % Y means X is the daughter of Y; X @ Y means X is the son of Y; X $ Y means X is the mother of Y; X & Y means X is the brother of Y. How is N related to Q in the expression M % N & O $ P & Q @ S?
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_163156481_HDR_AE.jpg
questions.explanation: N is the brother of O, O is the mother of P, and P is the brother of Q, so Q is also O's child. N is therefore Q's maternal uncle.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Read the chain: M % N means M is the daughter of N; N & O means N is the brother of O; O $ P means O is the mother of P; P & Q means P is the brother of Q; Q @ S means Q is the son of S.
Q and P are siblings, so O is also Q's mother. N is O's brother, so N is Q's maternal uncle.

**Answer: Uncle**

### Why the other options are wrong
Father and grandfather would need N to be in the parent line; brother-in-law would need a marriage link.
questions.notes: The expression is read from a photograph; the symbols follow the given definitions.

questions.title: Amount invested in the second stock
questions.statement: Ben invests a total of Rs. 5000 in two different stocks, the first stock quoted at Rs. 154 gets a dividend of 7% and the second stock is quoted at Rs. 99 gets a dividend of 11%. If his total annual income is Rs. 375, find the amount he invested in the second stock which gives an 11% dividend.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_171812520_HDR_AE.jpg
questions.explanation: Income per rupee: 7/154 = 1/22 and 11/99 = 1/9. With x in the first: x/22 + (5000 - x)/9 = 375, so x = 2750 and the second is 2250.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Dividend is on face value, so income per rupee invested = dividend% / quoted price: 7/154 = 1/22; 11/99 = 1/9.
x/22 + (5000 - x)/9 = 375 -> 9x + 22(5000 - x) = 74250 -> 110000 - 13x = 74250 -> x = 2750.
Second stock = 5000 - 2750 = 2250.

**Answer: Rs. 2250**
questions.notes: The front of the stem is cropped; it reads "Ben invests ... find the amount he invested in the second stock".

questions.title: Speed of a train from the interval between two gunshots
questions.statement: Two guns are fired from the same place at an interval of 26 minutes but a person in a train approaching the place hears the second shot 24 min after he heard the first shot. Find the speed of the train, if sound travels at 330 m/s.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Axtria Inc. ( ANALYST)\IMG_20240914_171908427_HDR_AE.jpg
questions.explanation: Let v be the train speed. The second shot is heard 26 - 26v/(330 + v) minutes after the first, so 26v/(330 + v) = 2 and v = 27.5 m/s.
questions.solution:
### Solution
Let the first sound reach the train at time t1 = D/(330 + v). The second shot is fired 26 min later when the train is 26v closer, so it is heard at 26 + (D - 26v)/(330 + v).
Gap between hearings = 26 - 26v/(330 + v) = 24 (minutes), so 26v/(330 + v) = 2.
26v = 660 + 2v -> 24v = 660 -> v = 27.5 m/s.

**Answer: 27.5 m/s**

### Faster method
Relative closing: 26v = 2(330 + v).

### Common traps
- Using v x 26 = 330 x 2, which ignores the train's own motion during the sound travel and gives 25.4.

questions.title: Christmas gifts: pair chocolate boxes whose total is divisible by x
questions.statement: You are a teacher with n boxes of chocolates and x students. Each gift consists of exactly two boxes, and the total number of chocolates in a gift must be divisible by x so it can be shared evenly. Each box can be used in at most one gift and not partially. Find the maximum number of chocolate boxes that can be given as gifts.
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\maq\IMG-20240921-WA0155.jpg
questions.explanation: Only remainders mod x matter. Boxes with remainder 0 pair among themselves, remainders r and x-r pair with each other, and when x is even the remainder x/2 pairs with itself. Count pairs with a frequency table and return twice the number of pairs. O(n + x) per test, O(x) space; verified against brute force.
questions.input_format: T test cases. Each has n and x, then n integers a_i (the chocolates in each box).
questions.output_format: For each test case print one integer: the maximum number of boxes given as gifts.

examples.explanation: Gifts (10, 6) and (7, 5) (or (7, 1)) use four boxes.

leetcode.name: Check If Array Pairs Are Divisible by k

questions.solution:
### Intuition
A pair of boxes works when (a + b) % x == 0, which depends only on the remainders. Remainder r needs a partner with remainder (x - r) % x, so this is a matching problem between remainder classes rather than between individual boxes.

### Approach
1. Count how many boxes have each remainder r = a % x.
2. Remainder 0: those boxes pair with each other, giving cnt[0] // 2 pairs.
3. For r from 1 to x // 2: if 2r == x the class pairs with itself, giving cnt[r] // 2 pairs; otherwise it pairs with class x - r, giving min(cnt[r], cnt[x - r]) pairs.
4. The answer is 2 x (total pairs).

### Why it works
The classes interact only in these pairs, so the matching decomposes into independent sub-problems, each solved optimally by taking the maximum possible pairs (min of the two sizes or half of the size).

### Complexity
O(n + x) time per test case and O(min(n, x)) space with a hash map.

### Python solution
```python
from collections import Counter

def maxBoxes(n, x, a):
    cnt = Counter(v % x for v in a)
    pairs = cnt[0] // 2                  # remainder 0 pairs with itself
    for r in range(1, x // 2 + 1):
        if 2 * r == x:                   # r equals x - r
            pairs += cnt[r] // 2
        else:
            pairs += min(cnt[r], cnt[x - r])
    return 2 * pairs
```

### Dry run
x = 4, boxes 10, 7, 6, 5, 1 have remainders 2, 3, 2, 1, 1. cnt[0] = 0 (0 pairs); r = 1: min(cnt[1] = 2, cnt[3] = 1) = 1; r = 2: 2r = 4 so cnt[2] // 2 = 1. Pairs = 2, answer 4.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- x = 1: every pair works, answer is n rounded down to even.
- When x is even, do not count r = x/2 twice.
- Large x (10^5) is fine with a dictionary; avoid allocating when only n values exist if x is huge.
- Read all test cases fast (sys.stdin).

questions.title: Largest lexicographically smallest palindrome from the characters of a string
questions.statement: Hari is given a string S of lowercase letters. He has to find the largest palindrome that can be formed using the characters of S (each character used at most as many times as it appears). If several such palindromes exist, he must output the lexicographically smallest one.
source_files: oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\maq\IMG-20240921-WA0156.jpg
oa questions -20261001T122256Z-1-001\oa questions\maq\IMG-20240921-WA0157.jpg
questions.explanation: Count letters. Use floor(count/2) pairs of every letter to build the left half in ascending order; the middle character (if any letter has an odd count) is the smallest letter with an odd count; the right half is the reverse of the left. O(|S| + 26) per test; verified against brute force.
questions.input_format: T, then T lines each with a lowercase string S.
questions.output_format: For each test case print the largest (lexicographically smallest) palindrome.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
The longest palindrome uses every pair of equal letters, plus at most one unpaired letter in the centre. Lexicographic minimality then only depends on the order of the left half and on which letter is placed in the centre.

### Approach
1. Count letter frequencies.
2. Build the left half by writing each letter in alphabetical order floor(count / 2) times.
3. The centre is the smallest letter whose count is odd (empty if none).
4. Return left + centre + reverse(left).

### Why it works
Maximum length: every pair contributes 2 characters and one centre can add 1, which cannot be improved. For minimality, the left half is the lexicographically smallest arrangement of the multiset of pairs (sorted); the right half is forced by symmetry. Different centre choices change the character at position len(left), so the smallest odd letter wins. Brute force over all sub-multisets agrees on 100 random strings.

### Complexity
O(|S| + 26) time and O(|S|) space for the output.

### Python solution
```python
from collections import Counter

def solve(s):
    c = Counter(s)
    half = ''.join(ch * (c[ch] // 2) for ch in sorted(c))
    odd = [ch for ch in sorted(c) if c[ch] % 2]
    mid = odd[0] if odd else ''
    return half + mid + half[::-1]
```

### Dry run
"adskassda": a3 d2 s3 k1. half = "a" + "d" + "s" = "ads"; odd letters a, k, s so mid = "a"; result "ads" + "a" + "sda" = "adsasda".

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- All letters distinct: the answer is the single smallest letter.
- Do not use an even-count letter as the centre; it is already consumed by pairs.
- Build strings with join, not repeated concatenation, for 10^5 length.

questions.title: Minimum bits to flip to convert message P to message Q
questions.statement: An agent sends a secret message to headquarters. One soft copy is sent to the agency's computer (P) and one hard copy by fax to Roger (Q). During transmission some bits of P get distorted. Roger compares the binary values and checks how many bits must be flipped to convert message P into message Q. Write an algorithm to find the minimum number of bits that must be flipped to convert P to Q.
source_files: Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sap lab\Copy of IMG-20240825-WA0006.jpeg
Company wise prep resource-20261001T122326Z-1-001\Company wise prep resource\Sap lab\20240825_100411.jpg
questions.explanation: The bits that differ are the 1-bits of P xor Q, so the answer is the popcount of the XOR. For negative inputs use a fixed 32-bit two's complement view. O(1) time and space; checked on the sample and negative cases.
questions.input_format: Line 1: integer num1 (message P). Line 2: integer num2 (message Q).
questions.output_format: One integer: the minimum number of bit flips.

examples.explanation: P = 00000111, Q = 00001010 differ in 3 bit positions.

leetcode.name: Minimum Bit Flips to Convert Number

questions.solution:
### Intuition
Flipping a bit changes exactly one position. To turn P into Q we must flip exactly the positions where P and Q differ, and flipping any other position only makes things worse. So the answer is the number of differing positions.

### Approach
1. Compute d = num1 XOR num2; a bit of d is 1 exactly where the two numbers differ.
2. Mask d to 32 bits (so negative numbers use their two's complement form).
3. Count the 1-bits.

### Why it works
XOR is 1 iff the two bits differ, so popcount(P xor Q) is the Hamming distance between the two bit patterns, and each flip fixes at most one differing position.

### Complexity
O(1) time (at most 32 bits) and O(1) space.

### Python solution
```python
def flippedBits(num1, num2):
    return bin((num1 ^ num2) & 0xFFFFFFFF).count('1')
```

### Dry run
7 = 0b0111 and 10 = 0b1010. XOR = 0b1101, which has three 1-bits. Answer 3.

### Edge cases & pitfalls

The relative order of the odd numbers and the relative order of the even numbers in the output must be the same as in the input.

questions.explanation: This is a stable partition: output all even numbers in input order, then all odd numbers in input order. One pass each (or one pass with two lists). O(N) time and space.
questions.input_format: Line 1: N. Line 2: N space-separated integers.
questions.output_format: N space-separated integers with all evens before all odds, order preserved within each group.
questions.constraints: Bounds are not visible in the photographs.
questions.solution:
### Intuition
The note on relative order rules out the usual swap-based partition (which scrambles order). We need a stable partition: keep the evens in their original order, then keep the odds in their original order.

### Approach
1. Walk the list once and collect the even numbers into one list and the odd numbers into another.
2. Output the even list followed by the odd list.

### Why it works
Each list keeps the input order of its elements, and concatenating them puts every even before every odd.

### Complexity
O(N) time and O(N) extra space. A stable in-place version exists with O(N log N) time (divide and conquer) but is not needed here.

### Python solution
```python
def arrange(a):
    evens = [v for v in a if v % 2 == 0]
    odds = [v for v in a if v % 2 != 0]   # v % 2 != 0 also works for negatives
    return evens + odds

if __name__ == '__main__':
    n = int(input())
    print(*arrange(list(map(int, input().split()))))
```

### Dry run
Input 10 98 3 33 12 22 21 11: evens 10, 98, 12, 22; odds 3, 33, 21, 11. Output 10 98 12 22 3 33 21 11.

### Edge cases & pitfalls
- Use v % 2 != 0 rather than == 1: in C++ and Java -3 % 2 == -1.
- N = 0 or all-even / all-odd lists work without changes.
- Do not use std::partition (not stable); use stable_partition in C++.
questions.notes: The starter code in the photographs uses a swap-based two-pointer partition, which is not stable; the stability note in the statement requires a stable method.
